articles.title_zh: Kindness returned: disabled Chinese man helps woman who aided him 8 years ago
articles.content_orig:
Over an 8-year friendship, Wang sent Zhu hometown produce and seafood annually, while Zhu sent clothes to his family every season
A Chinese woman donated 500 yuan (US$75) to an 18-year-old stranger with a disability after seeing a social media post saying he was too poor to afford meals.
Eight years later, he repaid her double the amount after learning she was going through a difficult time, which moved many people online.
In 2018, Wang Shuming, from China’s eastern Shandong province, posted a video saying he had no money and could not afford food.

articles.title_orig: Canada and Europe share challenge of diversifying without antagonizing US and China
articles.title_zh: Canada and Europe share challenge of diversifying without antagonizing US and China
articles.content_orig:
MONTREAL — There’s one thing the European Union and Canada want to avoid with their new alliance: stoking new fury from Washington and Beijing.
Officials have been under pressure to check off everything they said they would do at the last summit and on Friday will unveil the areas they plan to focus on over the next year, as they intensify their transatlantic cooperation. But don’t expect a parade of new deals.
“Canada has objectives where they need our technology — so you can build a beautiful relationship if you focus on it,” one senior EU official told POLITICO about shared challenges in diversifying away from the U.S. and China. The official was granted anonymity to speak candidly about sensitive diplomatic negotiations between Brussels and Ottawa.
One of the core EU interests in Canada, the official explained, is a chance for the bloc to diversify its supply of critical raw materials and sources of energy to further reduce its dependence on China and Russia, respectively.
“They have most of what we need,” the official said about Canadian minerals. “There’s also a huge opportunity to bring Canadian fossil fuels and gas to the EU.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed the controversy over whether the EU should label the relationship with Canada as an “associate membership,” saying on Thursday it was a sideshow to what’s been billed as a landmark summit.
Earlier this week, Germany, France, Greece and other countries opposed the definition in a joint EU-Canada statement to be issued in Montreal. That came after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen put forward the “associate membership” label in September.
But Carney told reporters on Thursday that the new alliance wasn’t “a marketing exercise” and that the name doesn’t matter. “What matters is that the complementarities of our two jurisdictions strengthen our sovereignty, strengthen Europe’s sovereignty, various strategic autonomies, critical minerals, energy, other aspects — AI,” he said.
A tricky political road lies ahead as Carney and von der Leyen make moves to draw the EU and Canada closer in a partnership that doesn’t include its southern neighbor. They’ll need to  tiptoe forward with an “association without accession” work plan in the last years of the U.S. President Donald Trump’s time in office.
Montreal’s historic Fairmont The Queen Elizabeth hotel was a hub of summit activity on Thursday, beginning with a morning spectacle of von der Leyen heading out of the hotel in runners, taking staff out for a walking meeting. EU commissioners and Canadian Cabinet ministers sailed in and out of the hotel’s perfumed lobby, greeting colleagues.
Jet-lagged Europeans, along with Canadian officials and lobbyists, commiserated over what they saw as poor summit organization, spread across multiple locations.
The debate over membership semantics became a luncheon laugh line when European Council President António Costa endorsed Von der Leyen’s offer to Canada before joking the final designation is “subject to revision”
Then, between servings of frisée salad and roast salmon, Costa struck a diplomatic balance.
“Tomorrow, the European Union and Canada will launch an alliance for the future of Europe,” he said, invoking German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s preferred label and a term Carney has also used to describe the relationship. But Costa also backed von der Leyen’s “ambition” of Canada as an “associate member” of the EU, admitting the term might not matter in the end.
By mid-afternoon, Carney seemed to come around to the term, recognizing the work underway to deepen relations as “an alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member, between Canada and the European Union.”
The two sides are expected to announce a wrap on talks on a new digital trade agreement on Friday, ending negotiations that were launched in the spring. Other anticipated outcomes include an agreement between the European Investment Bank and Canada, geared to allow the bloc to fund Canadian critical minerals projects.
Eleven EU commissioners in town to “further an agenda” is no small accomplishment, Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told reporters. “It’s a historic moment that we need to seize.”
AI and energy companies are expected to be major beneficiaries of an enhanced EU–Canada relationship, making the absences of European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen and Canadian Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson noteworthy.
Zoya Sheftalovich contributed to this report from Montreal.

articles.title_orig: Crypto worth billions frozen after suspected Binance hack
articles.title_zh: Crypto worth billions frozen after suspected Binance hack
articles.content_orig:
Several crypto firms, including Circle Internet Group and Tether, on Thursday froze $2.54 billion of funds tied to a potential hack on cryptocurrency exchange Binance.
The world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes didn't explicitly confirm that it has suffered an exploit.
"Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating," a Binance spokesperson said. "Rest assured that user funds are completely safe." Binance also said on X that Binance Alpha trading had been temporarily suspended, and that "the current verified total frozen is $2.54 billion."
Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao said in a post on X that user funds were safe and that he expected all customer funds to be fully covered. Zhao, who no longer runs the exchange, also said the incident appeared to be a hack.
Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said Thursday evening in a social media post that the company had frozen more than 800 million in USD Coin associated with the incident. USDT stablecoin issuer Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino also said in on X that his firm had frozen more than 1.5 billion of its stablecoin that may have been related to a potential breach.
Later, Binance co-founder Yi He said in a statement that the XRP and RLUSD-tied firm Ripple helped halt the movement of $200 million of funds linked to the possible attack.
But those frozen funds could represent only a fraction of the ones impacted. Crypto data provider Arkham Intelligence linked nearly $6 billion in digital assets — including bitcoin , ether , solana and various stablecoins — to 55 wallet addresses it has linked to the potential exploit.
Arkham identifies, tracks and flags crypto wallets by analyzing publicly available blockchain data. It also solicits tips from its community members.
Exploits are not uncommon in the crypto space. In 2025, Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to a hack. More recently, Bitget lost more than $350 million worth of digital assets in a cyber theft incident. Over the past several years, bad actors have also drained billions of dollars in crypto from decentralized exchanges.
Bitcoin — the most widely followed cryptocurrency in the world — slid more than 3% following the executives' statements, breaking below $80,000. Ether fell nearly 4%, while solana shed about 3%.
Shares of Circle also tumbled about 5% in after-hours trading on Thursday.

articles.title_orig: Amazon Spending Soars Amid Slowing Growth of Online Business
articles.title_zh: Amazon Spending Soars Amid Slowing Growth of Online Business
articles.content_orig:
Amazon's cloud-computing unit reported more rapid third-quarter growth than analysts had projected.
Revenue came in at $45.98 billion, up 39% year over year and above the $45.29 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount, according to a statement . Growth in the second quarter came in at about 37% .
"Our core compute and storage revenue grew at their fastest rates in several years," Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on a conference call with analysts. The AWS growth rate was the highest since the fourth quarter of 2021.
Amazon remains the top cloud by revenue, but growth has also sped up at rivals Alphabet and Microsoft. On Wednesday Alphabet said the Google Cloud business, which contains infrastructure and Google Workspace subscriptions, more than doubled in the third quarter.
All the major clouds have been racing to build data centers that can accommodate high artificial intelligence demand. During the quarter, AWS announced plans to expand its portfolio of Nvidia graphics processing units that can handle AI workloads.
AWS also acquired data analysis startup DuckLabs and signed deals with Meta and OpenAI, according to the statement.
The AWS segment generated $17.77 billion in third-quarter operating income, up 55% and more than the $16.97 billion StreetAccount consensus.
The unit now accounts for almost 23% of Amazon's revenue, a record.
On Wednesday, Microsoft published its first earnings report that contained revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars. Azure is 72% the size of AWS, up from 58% two years ago.
AWS came before Azure and the Google Cloud Platform, with its first services appearing in 2006.
"With our continued pace of innovation, new core and AI functionality, enterprises wanting to run their core and AI workloads in AWS, and the amount of capacity that we're adding each year, we believe that AWS can grow north of 40% in each of 2027 and in 2028, and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years," Jassy said.
Google has been pumping up its cloud revenue by making its tensor processing units for AI available outside its own facilities. Now Amazon will adopt the strategy with its Trainium chips for training models, starting in late 2027.
"With Trainium demand so strong, customers continue encouraging us to make it available outside of AWS. We intend to do so late in 2027," Jassy said.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu alleges stolen election as he seeks political survival amid uncertainty
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu alleges stolen election as he seeks political survival amid uncertainty
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Chief of Staff, Ido Norden, transferred information to the Israel Police that led to the arrests of three Arab Ra’am party activists on Tuesday on suspicion of election bribery, N12 News reported on Thursday.
The three Bedouin suspects, residents of the Segev Shalom and Ar’ara BaNegev communities, are suspected of attempting to bribe citizens on the eve of Election Day to vote for Ra'am.
According to N12, Norden called senior police officials and provided details that initiated the investigation and led to the arrests. Lahav 433 now has jurisdiction over the case.
Netanyahu called for a formal investigation following the arrests, saying that the suspects were "in possession of envelopes containing cash, along with ballots for [Ra'am party chairman] Mansour Abbas."
“Right-wing voters, dear Likud voters, in the face of attempts to compromise the integrity of the elections, you must go out and vote Mahal, vote Likud for the sake of our country!” Netanyahu said in response to the incident.
“We categorically reject attempts by elements within the police to link Ra’am to the compromising of electoral integrity,” the Ra’am party said in response. “The activists were arrested at their homes hours before the polls opened, not in the vicinity of polling stations or voters.”
“These are baseless arrests intended to undermine Ra’am and suppress voter turnout within Arab society, as part of [National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir’s political exploitation of Israel Police.”
Senior officials told N12 that the case is unlikely to lead to an indictment and that the suspects explained the source of the money in question.
Earlier on Thursday, Abbas denied claims that he was involved in a separate, alleged election interference scheme via Qatar, saying he backs an investigation into the matter and claiming that Netanyahu employs Qatari agents.
"Ra'am welcomes the decision of Central Elections Committee (CEC) Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg to investigate suspicions of an attempt to improperly influence the elections through foreign funding," said Abbas. "And to Abu Yair [Netanyahu], who employs Qatari agents in his office, we have one message in response to the campaign of incitement and delegitimization he is conducting against Arab citizens: 'There will be nothing, because there is nothing.' Unlike you, with us this is the truth and not another lie."
The Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) launched an investigation into suspicions that foreign entities, potentially including Qatar and Turkey, funneled money into Israel to influence voting in Arab communities.
The investigation, begun following a directive issued by Sohlberg, was initiated amid "severe suspicions... regarding improper influence through foreign funding by entities acting against Israeli interests during the elections," the Shin Bet stated.
Jonah Davidov and Corinne Baum contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Crypto firms freeze more than $2.5bn in funds as Binance investigates potential hack
articles.title_zh: Crypto firms freeze more than $2.5bn in funds as Binance investigates potential hack
articles.content_orig:
World’s largest crypto exchange said it had not confirmed whether funds had been pilfered
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday it is investigating reports of a potential security issue as its founder said the incident “does look like a hack on Binance”. The company said cryptocurrency firms had frozen about $3bn in funds by Thursday evening.
It was not immediately clear the extent of the damage hackers might have been able to accomplish and Binance had not explicitly confirmed that funds had been pilfered, but stablecoin issuers quickly froze funds Thursday evening.
“Our teams continue to work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” Binance said in a statement posted to social media. “User funds are safe.”
Stablecoin providers Tether and Circle each said they froze funds Thursday in response to the incident.
Jeremy Allaire, co-founder and CEO of Circle, wrote on X that the company had frozen more than an equivalent of $800m in currency associated with the incident “in coordination with law enforcement”. Paolo Ardoino, the CEO of Tether, said on X that the company froze the equivalent of more than $1.5bn in currency related to “a potential Binance exchange hack”.
The price of bitcoin dropped 3.2% Thursday afternoon to under $79,000.
Binance was founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who in 2023 pleaded guilty to a felony related to his failure to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as CEO. Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.
Zhao posted on X on Thursday that “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack on Binance”. He added that while he doesn’t manage Binance anymore, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”.

articles.title_orig: China Elevates Key Figure in Purges With Rare Politburo Pick
articles.title_zh: China Elevates Key Figure in Purges With Rare Politburo Pick
articles.content_orig:
Last week Beijing’s deputy mayor was meeting with Walmart CEO John Furner and encouraging American companies to invest in the Chinese capital. Now he has vanished from public life, the latest to be swept up in an anti-corruption campaign that has ensnared a galaxy of China’s talent: a former top judge, a spy chief, dozens of military generals – and even officials tasked with rooting out graft in the People’s Republic.
In hushed tones across China party officials are wondering who is next, as the purge continues to reach into the highest echelons of the ruling Communist Party and has even toppled those seen as being close to leader Xi Jinping.
The only person who doesn’t need to worry about their future is Xi himself.
Unlike US President Donald Trump , who is currently battling to save his party’s fortunes at the midterm elections and is constitutionally barred from serving more than two terms, Xi’s rule over the aspiring superpower and world’s second-biggest economy has never looked more secure.
He will take that confidence into a high-level closed-door meeting of more than 200 of the party elite in Beijing this week that is all set to further boost his authority – and his signature anti-corruption drive. Attendance at this meeting will be at a historic low – because of the anti-corruption measure.
The meeting is being particularly closely watched because it is held just a year before an even more important gathering of Communist Party leadership next fall where Xi is expected to engineer for himself an unprecedented fourth term.
The years-long anti-corruption campaign has ensured there are few, if any, figures or factions who could stand against him.
Since Xi, 73, came to power over 14 years ago millions of rank-and-file officials have been purged. In 2022, Xi called to “turn the blade inward” to investigate those tasked to enforce discipline themselves.
But he’s still not satisfied.
Earlier this year he told party cadres that the corruption problem “remains grave” and warned that there were still many “two-faced people” in the party. The war against graft, he promised, would be a “never-ending struggle.”
In recent months, the speed and scale of the anti-corruption drive have reached levels unseen in decades.
According to official data from the party’s Central Commission of Discipline Inspection (CCDI), between 2012 and 2022, over 500 ministerial-level officials have been probed, later convicted, removed from their posts, and expelled from the party for corruption.
In just the past three years, more than 410 officials have been purged.
Some of those purges have reached places that were once considered untouchable.
The party’s top military decision-making body, the usually seven-member Central Military Commission is now down to only two members – one of those being Xi himself . The 24-member politburo - the party’s top echelon - is down to only 21 members.
Over the past three weeks, ahead of the Beijing meeting, the CCDI has been sending out near daily updates of arrests, new probes and expulsions from the party.
The news that Huang Qifan was being probed sent shockwaves through political circles.
Huang was a longtime mayor of the megacity of Chongqing, known as a consummate political survivor who had served under six different secretaries of the Communist Party – and seen two of them go to jail, including a former rival of Xi.
In retirement, Huang was prolific at conferences and on TV, giving his takes on the Chinese economy.
Since his downfall, those who knew Huang have rushed to scrub all mention of their former well-connected friend and colleague from their social media accounts – a common practice in China.
For Beijing deputy mayor Xia Linmao, the purge came suddenly. Only days before, state TV showed him at a meeting with Walmart’s Furner and a slew of other US executives, nodding and taking his notes as his boss invited the group to do more business in Beijing.
Others simply vanished from public view, with news of their investigation not appearing for months, like Ma Xingrui, an aerospace engineer turned senior party official who once ran the vast western region of Xinjiang. The authorities announced an investigation into him in April – after he had not been seen in public for five months.
Being officially investigated for corruption almost always spells the end of a political career in China, with guilty officials kept from the public eye even after they have served their sentences.
And in recent months, authorities have shown they are willing to use capital punishment to enforce the party line, even for those who were once trusted aides of Xi.
In May, two former defense ministers, Wei Fenghe and Li Shangfu were given suspended death sentences, with a two-year reprieve , after being convicted of bribery.
Years of purging has left a generation of younger officials with fewer seniors left who can provide patronage, protection and career advancement, and the situation where the most powerful person in China does not have an apparent heir , in a break from his predecessors.
And for some, that’s just fine.
Deng Yuwen, a former deputy editor of the Study Times, the official publication of the party’s top training institute, told CNN that “now younger people all listen to Xi, isn’t this better? At this point, I don’t think Xi needs to worry about whether someone is already his trusted aides. “
“Whoever he promotes will become his loyalist,” said Deng. “And he has enough time to make someone his trusted loyalists.”

articles.title_orig: Chinese scholars warned of challenge of ‘translating research into policy’
articles.title_zh: Chinese scholars warned of challenge of ‘translating research into policy’
articles.content_orig:
A conference discussing the field known as ‘area studies’ said it was necessary to move beyond Western frameworks
Chinese academic courses designed to deepen understanding of different countries or regions face a challenge in better informing policy and moving beyond frameworks developed in the West, a conference in Beijing has heard.
Speakers said that as the country’s international engagement deepened, it needed a better understanding of the nations it engaged with, including their political systems, histories and strategic priorities.
The discipline – known in China as “area studies” – draws on disciplines including history, politics, economics and sociology to examine individual countries and regions.

articles.title_orig: Why Josh Kushner’s Firm Just Spent $7.6 Billion on a 150-Year-Old Company
articles.title_zh: Why Josh Kushner’s Firm Just Spent $7.6 Billion on a 150-Year-Old Company
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Home security company ADT ( ADT ) agreed on Thursday to be acquired and taken private by Thrive Holdings in an all-cash deal that values the company at $7.6 billion.
Thrive Holdings will pay $10 per share in cash for ADT, representing a 45.6% premium over ADT stock's closing price on Oct. 27.
ADT stock soared 34% to around $9.93 per share on the news, putting it on pace for its highest close since August 2021.
Thrive Holdings is a private capital group founded by Josh Kushner and backed by OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), focused on acquiring enterprise businesses for the long term and advancing their artificial intelligence and technological capabilities.
Thrive currently operates 75 businesses across accounting, IT services, and the built environment.
"ADT has spent generations showing up for people when it matters most," Thrive Holdings partner Kareem Zaki said in a press release . "We intend to build on that foundation by strengthening ADT's technology and product capabilities, with the capital and patience to invest over decades. Our ambition is to help ADT's teams better serve customers and offer a seamless service with more actionable information for the professionals responding."
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
This story is developing. Check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: Bukele's gang offensive goes abroad as El Salvador rushes troops to Haiti
articles.title_zh: Bukele's gang offensive goes abroad as El Salvador rushes troops to Haiti
articles.content_orig:
What could go wrong? For over a week, El Salvador has been quietly sending troops to Haiti, a project whose scale was only revealed publicly last night: More than 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers will be sent to the Caribbean nation, but their mission and mandate remain opaque.
The deployment is a wildcard in Port-au-Prince, a city of densely-inhabited hills where battle lines constantly shift between dozens of gangs and anti-gang groups, including foreign forces, neighborhood vigilantes, and mercenaries.
Two thousand soldiers is a significant arrival here. That’s more than Haiti’s entire army, and about a quarter of the urban footprint of the Haitian National Police. It’s about equal to the current staffing of the multinational UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) and far outnumbers the private military contractors on the Haitian government’s secretive “task force.”
But how do they fit into Haiti’s fractured security landscape? Who is paying for it? And what exactly is their mission? For now, the Salvadoran forces’ command structure has not been established, according to a source close to the matter.
Exclusive: Inside Erik Prince’s secretive operation taking on Haiti’s gangs
On Thursday evening, Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele posted online in Haitian Creole, announcing that the deployment to Haiti is “nearly completed” and that “90% of the expenses” would be shouldered by El Salvador.
“This is not an operation against the Haitian people nor an invasion of Haiti… Our only goal is to bring our four aviation technicians back home. Furthermore, we intend to teach a lesson to the gangs,” he wrote.
“Perhaps future generations of Haitians will remember us as friends who once came to help,” he added.
The missing air technicians, catalyst for this deployment, disappeared earlier this month after an apparent gang ambush. They had been working with the GSF in a noncombat role, according to Salvadoran officials. In the immediate aftermath, 100 special forces were sent to Haiti to assist in search and rescue operations — a precursor to the now expanded force.
Ten days later, local sources say it is unlikely that the missing four can be recovered. If Salvadoran forces cannot achieve that, they’ll likely seek other wins, perhaps joining one of several existing security forces for an extended push against the gangs in retaliation.
A communiqué released by Haitian interim leader Alix Didier Fils-Aimé on Wednesday night described a phone call with Bukele about the deployment and operational cooperation “within the framework of the GSF.”
A clue to their plans may eventually lie with the troops’ physical location; at time of reporting, the Salvadorans were not staying at the main GSF base in Port-au-Prince.
El Salvador sends troops to Haiti to rescue four service members
Bukele has argued that he has unique bona fides to address Haiti’s crisis. His government’s own hardline crackdown on gangs back home did restore peace to what was once the most violent country in the Western Hemisphere — though critics highlight his use of mass incarceration and accusations of widespread abuses.
In a message posted to X last week, he addressed the gangs in Haitian Creole: “There is still time to avoid this,” Bukele said. “Return our four countrymen to us alive and unharmed and everything will return to the way it was before the kidnapping.”
Most residents of Port-au-Prince would rather see dramatic change, after years of brutal gang violence that have driven over a million people from their homes. Just two hours from Florida’s coast, the city is terrorized by frequent gang kidnappings, rape and arson, all broadcast on social media.
On Thursday, Haitians nationwide were reminded again of just how much insecurity has put civil life on pause, with the news that long-deferred presidential elections are postponed yet again until next year.
But experts warn about the dangers of additional players on a crowded urban battlefield. “The situation is volatile and could become more violent with innocent people being harmed,” Bill O’Neill, the UN’s human rights expert for Haiti, said.
Romain LeCoeur, Haiti expert at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime, echoed the concern. “Haiti’s security response no longer rests on a single strategy, but on a juxtaposition of multilateral, national and private actors, each operating under its own rules,” he said.
“As long as no one can say who decides and who is accountable, every operation risks adding to the confusion rather than to security.”
Reporting contributed by CNN’s Merlin Delcid in El Salvador.

articles.title_orig: Putin says Russia is ‘ready for war’ with Europe in chilling threat
articles.title_zh: Putin says Russia is ‘ready for war’ with Europe in chilling threat
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Vladimir Putin has said that Russia ⁠is prepared ‌for a potential war with Europe in his latest threat, though ‌he claimed Moscow does not ‌want one.
The Russian president said his country supports any steps aimed at restoring relations with European countries, as he commented on his phone call with the leaders of Norway and Finland, which took place on Tuesday.
But in a chilling threat, he said that if tensions were to escalate too far, there would be no winners.
"First of all, we are ready, but we want no war with Europe”, Putin said.
“And if anyone wants it, let them prepare, but right now they have not achieved their goal to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia.
“And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that."
Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Stoere had held “frank and substantive” talks with the Russian president in a bid to influence the Kremlin’s position as the conflict in Ukraine rages on.
Putin said they had been right to make the call, despite criticism from some European capitals that the two were breaking ranks and protocol by speaking with Moscow directly.
Follow the latest updates on the Russia-Ukraine war here.
Stoere said he and ​Stubb had "stressed ⁠the importance of de-escalation,” and that both had voiced strong support for Ukraine.
But the move attracted criticism from their Nordic counterparts including Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen as they urged Europe’s leaders to “stick together” on Ukraine.
Swedish prime minister Ulf Kristersson said other European leaders also said they were not informed of the talks.
Putin added that Moscow did not want the Baltic ‌Sea to face ​a situation similar ‌to ⁠that in the ⁠Strait of Hormuz .
He said Russia wanted no impediments to navigation in the Baltic Sea and added that restricting communication could lead to a situation similar to that in the Strait since the outbreak of the US-Iranian conflict in February.
"Does someone ⁠want the same situation in the Baltic ⁠as in the Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz?" Putin said.
"I don't know. ‌We don't want ​that, but we will respond ‌to any challenge."
Also on Thursday, the UK’s former chancellor Rachel Reeves urged Brussels to seize control of £175 bn in frozen Russian assets to help Ukraine defend against Kremlin aggression in the face of “a desperate winter”.
In her first significant intervention since leaving government, the Labour MP told the European Union that “the time to act is now”, with Kyiv confronting a funding blackhole and Donald Trump seeking to pressure the embattled country “to cut a deal with Moscow”.
Earlier this week, defence secretary Wes Streeting said that Britain must be ready for war in 1,000 days as the government tells Britons to stock up on tinned food and bottles of water.
Writing in The Telegraph , Mr Streeting warned that the UK’s adversaries could be ready to attack the country in 2030.
A jet-powered Russian drone hit two trains stopped at a station in central Ukraine on Thursday, killing at least 13 people and injuring 10 others, officials said.
Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated southern Ukrainian city since Tuesday, despite remaining locked in war since Russia’s all-out invasion of its neighbour more than four years ago.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy described it as a “horrific attack” that struck passenger trains in Dnipro.
Previous efforts to secure ceasefires either never worked out or the truces quickly fell apart.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq close lower for first time in 4 days, but most stocks rise
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq close lower for first time in 4 days, but most stocks rise
articles.content_orig:
The major U.S. stock indices closed mostly lower Thursday, with the Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 both falling 1.38% . Alphabet was the standout loser among the megacap technology names, tumbling 12.64% , while Amazon declined 4.25% ahead of its earnings release.
However, the selling was far from universal. The Russell 2000 gained 1.01% , the NYSE Composite edged higher, and advancing stocks comfortably outnumbered decliners within the S&P 500. The headline indices told a weaker story than the average stock.
After the close, attention shifted to another round of earnings. The initial reactions supplied showed Intel down 20.17% and Amazon down 6.30% , keeping technology shares in focus heading into the next session.
Dow Industrial Average: Down 132.48 points, or 0.25%, at 52,342.62.
S&P 500: Down 23.44 points, or 0.30%, at 7,720.54.
Nasdaq Composite: Down 365.13 points, or 1.38%, at 26,184.72.
Russell 2000: Up 28.71 points, or 1.01%, at 2,859.22.
Nasdaq 100: Down 410.65 points, or 1.38%, at 29,402.51.
Despite the declines in the major headline indices, the supplied breadth figures showed:
Dow: 24 advancing stocks versus 6 declining.
S&P 500: 402 advancing versus 84 declining.
Nasdaq 100: 58 advancing versus 43 declining.
Nasdaq market: 1,643 advancing versus 1,602 declining.
NYSE Composite: 1,276 advancing versus 505 declining.
The S&P 500’s negative close alongside strong positive breadth is particularly revealing. It points to concentrated pressure in heavily weighted stocks, while many other constituents moved higher. Small caps also attracted buying, with the Russell 2000 outperforming the Nasdaq Composite by approximately 2.39 percentage points .
Three of the seven stocks finished higher, but Alphabet’s sharp decline stood out:
Meta: Up 1.96% at $624.52.
Apple: Up 1.48% at $348.91.
Microsoft: Down 0.16% at $530.14.
Tesla: Down 0.23% at $403.30.
Nvidia: Down 0.83% at $213.60.
Amazon: Down 4.25% at $243.79.
Alphabet: Down 12.64% at $283.82.
A slew of earnings were released after the close with Intel and Amazon the highlights. Both of those stocks are not fairing well after missing on Revenues.  Amazon missed on revenues and EPS.
Intel: Adjusted EPS $0.52 vs $0.41 expected (BEAT) ; revenue $16.50 billion vs $16.60 billion expected (MISS) . Shares trading down 17.44% .
Amazon: EPS $1.89 vs $1.97 expected (MISS) ; revenue $201.90 billion vs $202.20 billion expected (MISS) . Shares trading down 6.40% .
Gilead Sciences: Adjusted EPS $2.55 vs $2.19 expected (BEAT) ; revenue $8.30 billion vs $7.80 billion expected (BEAT) . Shares trading up 2.65% .
Sandisk: Adjusted EPS $49.51 vs $46.20 expected (BEAT) ; revenue $11.031 billion vs $10.639 billion expected (BEAT) . Shares trading up 2.15% .
Starbucks: Adjusted EPS $0.80 vs $0.72 expected (BEAT) ; revenue $9.10 billion vs $9.22 billion expected (MISS) . Shares trading down 0.33% .
Pinterest: Reported EPS $0.04 vs $0.49 expected (MISS on the supplied figures) ; revenue $1.17 billion vs $1.21 billion expected (MISS) . Shares trading down -8.89% .
A falling index does not mean most stocks declined. In a market-capitalization-weighted index, a sharp move in a large constituent can outweigh gains across many smaller companies. Today’s S&P 500 decline alongside strong positive breadth illustrates that distinction.
Earnings also need to be judged alongside the price reaction. Sandisk beat both supplied estimates but traded lower, while Intel’s EPS beat did little to support its shares. The headline result is one input. For traders, the next step is to see whether the initial reaction holds as trading develops.

articles.title_orig: Deadly disease sparks new CDC rule for US-bound flyers as major airlines seek delay
articles.title_zh: Deadly disease sparks new CDC rule for US-bound flyers as major airlines seek delay
articles.content_orig:
Infectious disease expert Dr. Tyler Evans explains why the CDC's new passenger questioning requirements could help prevent Ebola transmission.
Major U.S. and international airline groups are pushing back against a new Ebola-related travel requirement that will affect millions of people flying into the United States.
Beginning Nov. 3, all passengers on international flights to the U.S. will have to confirm that they have not been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the previous 21 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The requirement applies to everyone flying into or connecting through the U.S. — including American citizens, green card holders and airline crew members, the CDC said.
US ISSUES URGENT TRAVEL WARNING AS DEADLY EBOLA OUTBREAK SPREADS OVERSEAS
Travelers will have to complete a paper or digital statement before boarding, even if they have never visited the DRC.
Airlines must collect the forms and keep them for at least 42 days after the flight arrives in the U.S., according to the CDC.
Beginning Nov. 3, all passengers on international flights to the U.S. will have to confirm that they have not been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the previous 21 days. (Megan Varner/Getty Images)
Airlines for America (A4A), which represents major carriers including American, Delta, Southwest, United and JetBlue, is asking the CDC to reconsider the requirement and give airlines more time to prepare, according to an Oct. 26 letter provided to Fox News Digital.
The group said it supports the CDC's public health goals but argued that the new requirement is too broad and is being introduced too quickly.
"We have to ensure that this does not cross borders."
A4A asked the government for a "more proportionate and measured U.S. response" focused more closely on affected areas and travelers who have recently been there.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The group also asked for the Nov. 3 start date to be delayed.
"Changes to check-in systems, digital signatures, station procedures and training cannot readily be completed in the allotted time," A4A wrote.
Dr. Tyler Evans, a California-based infectious disease physician and CEO of Wellness Equity Alliance, told Fox News Digital, "This was a step in the right direction, given the fact that we really do have to take this seriously. We have to ensure that this does not cross borders."
The new requirement applies to everyone flying into or connecting through the U.S., including American citizens, green card holders and airline crew members. (Ting Shen/Bloomberg)
He added, "This is the second-largest outbreak of Ebola in history. So this is very serious."
The International Air Transport Association (IATA), which represents more than 370 airlines around the world, has also asked the CDC to reconsider the requirement, Reuters reported.
"This is the second-largest outbreak of Ebola in history."
"It is unreasonable for the U.S. government to require all airlines serving the U.S. market to modify their procedures to accommodate the collection of attestations from each individual (passenger and crew) flying to the United States in less than two weeks," IATA wrote in a letter, according to Reuters.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES
A4A is also asking the CDC to exempt airline crew members, arguing that existing aviation documents already contain information about crews and their travel.
The group has requested an exemption for U.S. military passenger charters as well, saying the military already tracks service members' health, safety and whereabouts.
The CDC said the requirement is intended to reduce the risk of Ebola entering the United States through air travel.
U.S. and international airline groups are pushing back against a new CDC Ebola-related travel requirement. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The 21-day period reflects the maximum amount of time it can take for symptoms to appear after exposure.
Anyone who has been in the DRC during that period, including travelers who only passed through an airport there, will not be allowed to board a U.S.-bound flight unless they have a government exemption, the CDC said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Some of the initial symptoms would just be flu-like symptoms . You'll have a high-grade fever, you'll feel sort of fatigued," the doctor said.
"[For] people that ... are asymptomatic, being able to screen is a very effective modality to reduce, to prevent or mitigate further transmission," Evans said.
"Being able to screen is a very effective modality to reduce, to prevent or mitigate further transmission."
Evans worked on the Ebola response twice in the past, both in West Africa and in the DRC, the two largest outbreaks in history.
"The reality is Ebola is one of the most infectious and has one of the highest case fatality rates of infectious diseases ," Evans said.
But Americans often don't view Ebola as being relevant to them, he said. "When it comes to infectious diseases ... microbes don't sort of respect boundaries."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Travelers who knowingly provide false information could face prosecution and fines, according to the CDC.
Fox News Digital reached out to the CDC and IATA for further information and comment.

articles.title_orig: 'We're technically homeless': Residential cruise ceases operations
articles.title_zh: 'We're technically homeless': Residential cruise ceases operations
articles.content_orig:
More than 200 passengers, mostly Americans, are stranded in Cambodia after the operator of a luxury U.S. cruise ship that was on a continuous around-the-world voyage ran out of money due to skyrocketing fuel costs .
Villa Vie Residences, the Florida-based operator of the MV Odyssey, said the war with Iran quadrupled fuel costs and forced it to suspend operations on Tuesday.
CEO Mikael Petterson told CBS News in a phone interview Wednesday that Villa Vie Residences was paying an average of $700 a ton for fuel before the war broke out in late February. Since then, it has been paying anywhere from $2,000 to $3,000 per ton.
The Odyssey uses between 700 and 800 tons per month in fuel, Petterson disclosed.
"When you divide it over 300 people on board, it's just backbreaking," Petterson told CBS News. "And this has been going on for nine months. We've tried to do everything we can do."
In a statement, Villa Vie Residences said the per cabin fuel costs rose from an average of $1,800 per month before the war to between $6,000 and $8,000.
The company was unwilling to pass those rising costs on to its passengers, Petterson said.
The Odyssey launched in October 2024 for a continuous around-the-world journey. At the time, passengers could become residents of the ship by purchasing a permanent cabin for several hundred thousand dollars. Some sold their homes to do so. At the time, they were given a 15-year minimum guarantee of residency aboard the Odyssey.
The Odyssey attempted to counter the spiking fuel prices by slowing down its itinerary and spending five or six days in each port "hoping that things would come to a close in the Middle East," Petterson said, but it wasn't enough.
"For us, when our monthly expenses go up from $400,000 to $2 million, where are we going to get the $1.6 million?" Petterson asked.
The Villa Vie Residences CEO said that the ship ran out of money as it searched for a financial partner, and the plan is now to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
"We've borrowed money, we've stretched our payrolls as far as we can, and we're at a point where it's just at a breaking point where we need capitalization," Petterson said.
Passenger Benjamin Schatz thought the MV Odyssey would be his forever home.
"Honestly, right now, I'm in denial and in shock, and I'm heartbroken," Schatz, a retiree, told CBS News.
CBS News met Schatz in April 2025 for a story featuring Villa Vie Residences. At that point, he had been living on the ship for about one year. On Wednesday, he was given just hours to pack up his life and leave.
Said Schatz: "There are people now who are homeless and who have very little money and don't know what they're going to do."

articles.title_orig: Dow loses 100 points, S&P 500 snaps 3-day advance as Alphabet and Caterpillar tank: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow loses 100 points, S&P 500 snaps 3-day advance as Alphabet and Caterpillar tank: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Alphabet shares plunged the most since Google went public in 2004, dropping 13% on Thursday, wiping out roughly $500 billion in market cap.
In its earnings announcement late Wednesday, Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion for the third quarter, compared to the $2.7 billion analysts expected. The Google parent maintained its full year capital expenditure guidance of between $195 billion and $205 billion.
Microsoft , meanwhile, traded largely flat as investors focused on the tech giants' latest spending and free cash flow numbers in the third-quarter earnings report.
Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, which was 30% higher than a year ago, but below analyst projections of $50.67 billion. Free cash flow fell 27% to $18.63 billion but remained positive.
The earnings reports come as investors scrutinize AI spending plans of tech companies and are focusing on the returns on those investments.
"Microsoft is building out its architecture in a measured way and as such contains fewer surprises," Ben Barringer, global head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said on Thursday. "Alphabet, by contrast, saw its share price hit after hours as a result of a fairly messy set of results and a poorly handled earnings call" .
Alphabet's biggest source of revenue, search advertising, grew 12% in the September quarter to $63.35 billion, but missed analyst expectations, adding further pressure to the company's shares.
Philipp Schindler, Alphabet's chief business officer, said the impact on the search business was partly because of lower monetization within the company's AI Mode. He added that Alphabet is now "scaling" ads within its AI Overviews and AI Mode products, including in international markets.
Google's search business has faced headwinds from the rise of other AI chatbots like OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. People may be carrying out more search queries outside Google. Gemini, Google's own AI chatbot, has failed to keep pace.
"The problem for Google is it faces an innovator's dilemma and doesn't know whether to protect its core business or look to join the disruption. As such, Google has lost its edge with Gemini and is behind peers on agentic AI," Barringer said.
Google's dominant market share in the search business, however, could ultimately give it a leg up over its peers, Rosenblatt Securities analyst Scott Devitt said.
"I don't think it's a sea change," Devitt told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday. "If it's a problem for Alphabet, it's a problem for any consumer-facing AI agent or LLM as well. And so, it's a problem that I think is ultimately going to be resolved. And when it does, Alphabet, with its 4 billion search customers that become AI customers, is in an enviable position."
- CNBC's Robert Hum, Samantha Subin, Jordan Novet and Caleigh Keating contributed reporting.

articles.title_zh: Rivian Beats Estimates as R2 SUV Becomes Its Top-Selling EV
articles.content_orig:
Rivian Automotive beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations as it ramped up production of its new R2 entry-level SUV that the company has promised investors will lead it to profitability.
Here's how Rivian performed in the period ended Sept. 30, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
Shares of Rivian were up roughly 7% during afterhours trading Thursday, after hitting a new 52-week low of $11.38 earlier in the day. The stock closed at $11.45 a share, down 1.9%
The electric vehicle maker also revised its 2026 guidance to mark expected improvements in its vehicle deliveries, pre-tax adjusted earnings and capital expenditures.
The new guidance calls for a pre-tax adjusted loss of between $1.75 billion and $1.85 billion — a $100 million improvement at the midpoint from its prior guidance — vehicle deliveries of between 67,000 and 70,000 units, up from at least 65,000; and capital expenditures of between $1.4 billion and $1.5 billion, $300 million less at the midpoint.
Rivian attributed the improvement in its pre-tax adjusted earnings guidance to better-than-expected revenue related to its sales of regulatory credits, an IEEPA tariff refund receivable in the third quarter and its expected increase in vehicle deliveries.
The R2 — the first deliveries of which arrived to customers in June — has become Rivian's best-selling model and was responsible for "much of the gain quarter-over-quarter," the company said.
Rivian delivered a record 19,248 units from July through September. The company does not disclose deliveries by vehicle.
The EV maker remains unprofitable overall but continued to narrow its losses during the quarter. The company reported a net loss attributable to common stockholders of $913 million, compared with a loss of $1.17 billion during the third quarter of 2025.
Rivian's gross profit, which is closely monitored by investors, was $176 million during the third quarter, up from $24 million a year earlier. Its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was a loss of $435 million, a $167 million improvement from the same period last year.
The company reported that its software and services segment continues to grow, generating $605 million in revenue and a gross profit of $256 million, a 42% margin. That compares to its automotive operations, which recorded nearly $1.55 billion in revenue and a gross loss of $80 million.
Also on Thursday, Rivian reiterated that it expects the R2, a smaller and less expensive sibling to its current luxury R1S SUV, to have a positive gross margin by the end of the year. CEO RJ Scaringe has said the company needs to scale beyond current R2 production plans of 160,000 units in order to achieve overall profitability.
"That ramp-up is critical for us getting to positive gross margin on R2 and that ultimately will contribute to positive gross margin for the business," Scaringe told CNBC's Phil LeBeau during an interview Thursday. "We're going to see that through the end of the quarter and the unit economics will continue to grow … into Q1 of next year as well."
Rivian on Thursday said its cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments balance was $5.5 billion, up from $5.3 billion to end the second quarter.

articles.title_zh: Opinion | Can Canada, UK and Australia grasp chance offered by US-China rivalry?
articles.content_orig:
As the US shifts away from its commitment to global primacy, these Anglosphere nations have the potential to be a pivotal force for global stability
As middle powers, Australia, Britain and Canada can do more than most other nations to influence global peace in the face of a new great power rivalry between China and the United States. These three nations owe their citizens, and perhaps the wider world, an earnest effort to rise to the challenge of being peacemakers.
They have three attributes in common that give them unique potential to be a pivotal force. First is their own shared histories as members of the Anglosphere and therefore close allies of the US. Second is the recent US impetuousness and erratic behaviour towards the three of them, which demands greater independence and balance in their international relationships. Third is their shared middle power status, affording them enough diplomatic, military and trade significance to have great influence.
Today, though, Australia’s, Britain’s and Canada’s results as agents for global stability are mixed.

articles.title_orig: Ukrainians recount torture at hands of Russia’s sadistic ‘Dr. Evil’: ‘You can’t call him a human being’
articles.title_zh: Ukrainians recount torture at hands of Russia’s sadistic ‘Dr. Evil’: ‘You can’t call him a human being’
articles.content_orig:
Surviving Ukrainian prisoners of war have given sickening accounts of their torture at the hands of “Doctor Evil,” a notorious Russian medic at the heart of Vladimir Putin’s modern-day gulag system.
Operating out of Russia’s penal facility No. 10 in Mordovia, southeast of Moscow, Ilya Sorokin, 35, has been charged with torturing at least 29 Ukrainian PoWs in absentia by Ukraine’s SBU security service.
One former PoW described how the sadistic doctor would order them to strip off before subjecting them to cruel and degrading acts.
“There were 30 of us, all naked, in a room. He asked who had asthma, tuberculosis, or anything else,” Serhii Doroshenko, a Ukrainian military doctor, told the Times of London .
“But if, God forbid, you mentioned any illness, then he would torture you personally, on top of the torture from the prison staff, because you were making extra work for him,” Doroshenko added, speaking from his hospital bed, where he is still recovering from his injuries.
Doroshenko, captured during a battle for the eastern city of Mariupol in 2022, spent more than 1,000 days in Russian captivity before his release last year in a prisoner exchange.
“He kicked us and hit us with a baton and a stun gun. He knows where it hurts the most, and he deliberately strikes you right there,” Doroshenko said.
He described how Sorokin allegedly reserved his worst punishments for captured Ukrainian medical personnel, over unproven claims that they had carried out medical experiments on Russian troops.
“This myth was spread by Russian propaganda. They told us that in Mariupol medics ran some biological experiments on Russian soldiers and colonels,” Doroshenko said.
“That they had cut off their testicles. This is bulls–t, of course, but we got beaten for this just as much as artillerymen and snipers,” he added.
Other PoWs described how Sorokin, also nicknamed Dr Shocker, would wear a medical mask and sometimes a balaclava with a skull on it during the torture.
“You can’t call him a human being. He started to wave the stun gun around and shocked me several times,” Ukrainian marine infantry officer Pavlo Afisov told RFE/RL.
“He said we were ‘stinking khokhkly [A Russian slur for Ukrainians]’ who did not deserve decent treatment,” Afisov added.
Sorokin is also accused of using a stun gun on Ukrainian PoWs if they failed to shout “Glory to Russian medicine!” or if they asked for help with heart pains, festering wounds, or even a toothache.
Ukrainian inmates were ordered to address Sorokin with their heads down and their hands behind their backs, although some caught glances at his face, Doroshenko said.
“To raise your face was to die, or to receive so many blows that you might not survive,” he said.
The European Union has imposed sanctions on Sorokin, citing his “inhumane and degrading treatment” of prisoners.
Sorokin has denied the allegations against him.
He is far from the only Russian medic accused of torturing Ukrainian PoWs.
Hundreds of former prisoners have recounted witnessing Russian medical professionals “directly participating in torture, ill treatment, and the degrading treatment of detainees,” as part of a new report, “The Anatomy of Torture,” by the Kyiv-based Center for Civil Liberties.

articles.title_orig: Subcutaneous Toripalimab Plus Disitamab Vedotin sNDA Is Accepted in China for HER2-Expressing Urothelial Cancer
articles.title_zh: Subcutaneous Toripalimab Plus Disitamab Vedotin sNDA Is Accepted in China for HER2-Expressing Urothelial Cancer
articles.content_orig:
China's National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) has accepted a supplemental new drug application seeking the approval of a subcutaneous formulation of toripalimab (Loqtorzi; JS001sc) in combination with disitamab vedotin (Aidixi) as first-line treatment for patients with HER2-expressing locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma. 1 The application covers tumors with a HER2 immunohistochemistry score of 1+, 2+, or 3+.
With this filing, the NMPA has now accepted applications for subcutaneous toripalimab across all 13 indications for which intravenous toripalimab is approved in China. The agency accepted applications for 12 of those indications in March 2026, making JS001sc the first domestically developed subcutaneous anti–PD-1 monoclonal antibody in China to reach the new drug application stage.
In May 2026, the NMPA approved intravenous toripalimab plus disitamab vedotin for first-line treatment of HER2-expressing locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma, marking the 13th approved indication for toripalimab in mainland China. 2 Toripalimab had previously been approved in China in 2021 for advanced urothelial carcinoma in the second line or later.
The regulatory decision for the frontline combination was based on findings from the phase 3 RC48-C016 trial (NCT05302284), which enrolled patients at 74 centers across China.
RC48-C016 was a multicenter, open-label, randomized phase 3 trial in which 484 patients with previously untreated HER2-expressing locally advanced or metastatic urothelial cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to disitamab vedotin plus toripalimab every 2 weeks or gemcitabine plus cisplatin or carboplatin every 3 weeks. 3
Progression-free survival (PFS) by blinded independent review and overall survival (OS) served as dual primary end points, and secondary end points included objective response and safety.
At a median follow-up of 18.2 months, the median PFS was 13.1 months with the combination vs 6.5 months with chemotherapy (HR, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.28-0.46; P < .001). Additionally, the respective median OS values were 31.5 vs 16.9 months  (HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.41-0.73; P < .001). The objective response rate (ORR) was 76.1% (95% CI, 70.3%-81.3%) vs 50.2% (95% CI, 43.7%-56.7%).
Median duration of response was 14.6 months with the combination vs 5.6 months with chemotherapy. 2
Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse effects (AEs) occurred in 55.1% of patients in the combination arm and 86.9% of those in the chemotherapy arm. 3
Toripalimab is an anti–PD-1 monoclonal antibody that blocks the interaction between PD-1 and its ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2, and also induces internalization of the PD-1 receptor. Disrupting this signaling helps restore the immune system’s ability to recognize and attack tumor cells. 2
Disitamab vedotin is a HER2-directed antibody-drug conjugate composed of a humanized antibody, a protease-cleavable linker, and the cytotoxic payload monomethyl auristatin E. After binding to HER2 and being internalized by tumor cells, the conjugate releases its microtubule-disrupting payload. The combination therefore pairs targeted cytotoxic delivery with immune checkpoint inhibition.
Evidence for subcutaneous toripalimab has been derived from the phase 3 JS001sc-002-III-NSCLC study (NCT06505837), which compared subcutaneous with intravenous toripalimab, each given with chemotherapy, in patients with recurrent or metastatic nonsquamous non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). 1 The study met its primary end point in November 2025. In an oral presentation at the 2026 European Lung Cancer Congress, investigators reported that toripalimab exposure with the subcutaneous formulation was noninferior to that of the intravenous version, with similar efficacy and safety.
JS001sc-002-III-NSCLC is an open-label, randomized, multicenter phase 3 trial comparing the pharmacokinetics, efficacy, and safety of subcutaneous and intravenous toripalimab, each combined with chemotherapy, as first-line therapy for recurrent or metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC. 4
Patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to subcutaneous toripalimab 360 mg or intravenous toripalimab 240 mg, each given every 3 weeks, along with pemetrexed and cisplatin or carboplatin for 4 cycles. Those whose disease had not progressed then received maintenance pemetrexed with their assigned toripalimab formulation, with total toripalimab treatment capped at 35 cycles.
The study’s primary end points were the observed serum trough concentration at the end of cycle 1 and the model-predicted area under the concentration-time curve from day 0 to day 21 of cycle 1. Secondary end points included ORR, PFS, 6-month PFS rate, disease control rate, duration of response, and safety, which was assessed through AEs and abnormal laboratory parameters.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spy
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China , prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.
after newsletter promotion
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. Megaspeed and customers like it “receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security”.

articles.title_orig: Audio recordings reveal decisions made moments before deadly train crash in Spain
articles.title_zh: Audio recordings reveal decisions made moments before deadly train crash in Spain
articles.content_orig:
New audio obtained by Spanish media reveals that the operator of a stopped train called a control center to say she could not restart the train as another behind it sped ahead in its direction. The resulting crash of the two high-speed trains Wednesday killed at least 69 people and injured dozens more. As of Thursday, 67 passengers remained missing, according to Spanish officials.
Many questions remain about the failures that led to one of Spain’s worst transportation disasters in decades and whether something could have been done to prevent it. Audio recordings of communications between the train operators and staff members at a control center in Madrid shed light on the decisions made in the minutes before the trains collided.
Spain’s transportation minister, Óscar Puente, said Wednesday that a security system stopped working because of a computer malfunction, causing multiple trains on the line to stop at about 8:30 a.m. local time. With the computer system down, rail traffic was then handed over to the control center in Madrid.
At about 8:36 a.m., the control center authorized a state-owned Renfe high-speed train to resume its journey, without speed limitations, even though a stationary ‌train from the private rail company Iryo was on the tracks ahead, Puente said. An erroneous ​decision was ‌made ⁠to restart the ⁠Renfe train, breaking protocol, he said.
Audio obtained by Spanish media of the conversations between the operators of both trains and the control center sheds light on the series of decisions leading up to the collision at about 8:53 a.m., near the train station in Urda. NBC News has not been able to independently verify the authenticity of the audio.
After the computer system went down, the control center told the Renfe train operator to resume its journey “at normal speed,” according to an audio clip.
“At normal speed? OK,” the operator responded.
“OK, we’ll talk later,” the controller said before signing off.
Several minutes later, someone from the control center called the Iryo train to authorize it to also continue on its normal journey, according to an audio clip.
The operator of the Iryo train, which was ahead of the Renfe train, called back seven minutes later to say she had been unable to restart it. “I’m still stopped at the entrance signal,” she said, according to the audio clip. The control center told her to restart the train when she could and to call back if she had further problems, according to the audio. Several minutes later, the Renfe train ran into the back of the Iryo train.
The crash, the second deadly high-speed rail train collision this year in Spain, sent shock waves across the country. Until recently, the high-speed rail network was considered one of Spain’s crowning achievements. The crash came just weeks ahead of a major election in Spain, and it has led to criticism of the government and protests.
In January, a separate disaster on the same rail line killed 46 people. Several days later, a commuter train near Barcelona derailed, killing the driver and injuring dozens of other people.
Hundreds of emergency workers, firefighters, police officers and soldiers responded to the scene of Wednesday’s crash to rescue survivors and recover bodies. Cranes were brought in to move parts of the damaged trains later in the day.
Spain has the largest high-speed rail network in Europe for trains moving at more than 155 mph, with more than 1,900 miles of track, according to the European Union.
The identities of victims have begun to emerge.
Fátima Báñez, a former minister, was among those killed in the collision, according to the leader of Spain’s opposition Popular Party.
“She was a tireless woman, a loyal friend, and always committed to improving the lives of Spaniards,” Alberto Núñez Feijóo wrote in Spanish on social media .
Antonio Acedo, the driver of one of the trains, was also killed, according to the Izquierda Española political party.
“Antonio was an exceptional person, a kind, prudent, and dedicated man,” the party wrote on social media .
The country is observing three days of mourning after the crash.
Dirk Llorens, an American who lives in Madrid, said he and his wife were on the stopped train when, suddenly, “I was thrown just violently, just over my table.”
“Then the train started sliding, and I could see that the roof had opened, and there was dust flying out of the back,” he said.
People were panicking and did not know what had just happened, he said. Llorens thought the train had derailed somehow. He turned and saw that “everything was destroyed.”
Llorens said that as he and his wife tried to escape from the train, he saw people who had “smashed their face” during the impact, with bloody noses and cuts on their heads spewing blood.
He said that the crash occurred on a hill and that “we were all just trying to get out because we thought the train would roll on the hill and kill us.”
As more injured people escaped from the train, Llorens saw a man “come out completely full of blood, and he was just sitting on a tree, just completely collapsed.”
“I think people were so in shock. We were all in shock,” he said.
Those who were less injured began trying to help one another, he said, adding that soon afterward, a large group of paramedics and police arrived.
“You really never know what can happen in life — that makes you appreciate life but also understand that some things can happen at any time,” Llorens said.
He called for transparency from the Spanish government about what happened.
“The Spanish government really needs to put all their effort in making sure that something like that doesn’t ever happen again,” he said. “I don’t think I’ll take a train in Spain unless I see that they’re having big improvements in what they’re doing.”
Daniella Silva is a national reporter for NBC News, focusing on immigration.
Hernan Muñoz is a freelancer based in Spain.

articles.title_orig: Apple VP talks new iPad mini: OLED without ProMotion, Acoustic Display, more
articles.title_zh: Apple VP talks new iPad mini: OLED without ProMotion, Acoustic Display, more
articles.content_orig:
Apple unveiled its “biggest update ever” for the iPad mini this week, introducing a thinner, lighter design and an OLED display.
In a pair of interviews, Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering, discussed the new iPad mini’s design, display, and more.
About ProMotion: yeah right, OLED has faster response, hence why 60Hz is always enough. Oh wait... What about the iPad Pros, iPhone Pros and MacBook Pros with OLED at 120Hz?
While the new iPad mini features an OLED display, it doesn’t support ProMotion. Instead, it’s limited to a 60Hz refresh rate. Here’s what Pakula had to say about that decision in an interview with Chris Lawley :
Display experience is about more than just a single spec. One of the things that’s really cool about OLED is it actually has this really fast pixel response time. So it’s more than an order of magnitude faster than the pixel response time for an LCD display.
What that does is it makes everything really smooth. Motion blur is significantly reduced compared to LCD. When you pair that with the other things, the contrast, the brightness, and the color, this is just a killer display.
In addition to being lighter and thinner, the new iPad mini is also IP67-rated for water and dust resistance, a first for an iPad. One key enabler is a new Acoustic Display. Pakula explains how that technology works:
One of the cool things we realized as we started experimenting was that the unique size and form factor of this display actually had a resonant frequency that’s in the audible range.
I think more importantly, it’s in the range of like a traditional woofer that you’d have in a speaker. What we did was we built these custom drivers that actually energize the display and emit sound directly through the enclosure, but that only really works for the mid and low frequencies.
For the higher frequencies, we actually designed these little custom tweeters. There’s one on each end of the product, and they’re actually ported out through these hidden ports between the glass and the aluminum. The result is we have this product that’s water and dust resistant. I think the sound that comes from it is so surprising for a form factor of this size.
Pakula also sat down with Katarina Mogus for an interview , where he discussed how the iPad mini fits into a world where iPhone Duo also exists:
What we love about the iPad mini is it’s really the full iPad experience in the palm of your hand. That gives you access to a million+ apps in the App Store. It’s got incredibly powerful creative accessories like the Apple Pencil Pro. And it’s got the advanced multitasking of iPadOS 27.
It is really incredibly universal. And honestly, with all these updates, all of those experiences just got so much better.
You can watch both interviews below. The new iPad mini is available to pre-order now , with the first orders arriving on November 6.

articles.title_orig: EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit
articles.title_zh: EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit
articles.content_orig:
European Union and Canadian leaders are set to meet at a special Canada-EU summit to discuss critical policies like artificial inteligence (AI), climate, energy and ⁠security.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Thursday, ahead of the summit, which begins on Friday, that the EU will continue to explore Canada's prospects for becoming the bloc's first "associate member."
But despite her comments, the summit's declaration is expected to exclude the term "associate member," a move pushed by Germany and other members.
"Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession," Von der Leyen clarified. "We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before."
"We both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible," von der Leyen added.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had said this week he wasn't concerned about the  "associate member" status, or "specific names" to be given to the new alliance with the EU .
"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians," Carney added.
Ottawa's quest for deeper ties to Europe is seen as a move to reduce its reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods .
Frederic Merand, political expert on EU-Canada relations at the University of Montreal, spoke to DW about how the summit serves as "political impetus" to improve the bilateral trade relationship and to free Canada of its reliance on the US.
"It's not going to happen, over time, overnight. And every time we move closer to the Europeans, we realize how dependent we are on the US and how also vulnerable we are to, for example, us retaliation," Merand said.
But he added that courting the EU is also part of a broader strategy "to reinvent the Canadian economy, to create a single market, to attract more investment," as well as to diversify our partnerships with China, India and also other parts of the world.
The EU is "a natural partner" to work with, Merand said, given its existing free trade agreement with Canada, in addition to the close historical and cultural ties between the two partners.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Canada and the EU sought to align policies in areas such as climate, energy and artificial intelligence, allowing Ottawa to participate in some EU programs.
Canada has critical minerals needed for green technologies such as batteries and wind turbines, something for which Europe normally relies on China.
But Canada is in need of major infrastructure investment to develop its mining industry.
There are hopes that the summit can result in a plan for the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.
EU and Canadian leaders are also looking into a digital trade deal that can allow for faster and cheaper online transactions.
Additionally, Canada could be allowed to participate in the EU's Erasmus youth program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad.

articles.title_orig: King Charles arrives in Guyana as Bahamas visit declared 'diplomatic success'
articles.title_zh: King Charles arrives in Guyana as Bahamas visit declared 'diplomatic success'
articles.content_orig:
King Charles has arrived in Guyana for the second leg of his Caribbean tour, following a visit to the Bahamas which Buckingham Palace described as a "sensitive balancing act" and "diplomatic success".
The main themes of the two-day state visit to Guyana will be the environment and sustainability - alongside the growing commercial ties between the UK and Guyana.
The King is due to have an audience with the country's President, Irfaan Ali, and will attend a state reception celebrating the 60 year bilateral relationship between the two countries.
After visiting Guyana, King Charles will visit Antigua and Bermuda where he will open a major Commonwealth leaders summit in his role as the head of the "family of nations".
Guyana - formerly British Guiana - is the world's fastest growing economy due to the discovery of oil reserves there in 2015.
More than four fifths of Guyana is covered by rainforest and it has one of the lowest rates of deforestation in the world.
Cultural exchanges will also feature with a group of bagpipers from the National Piping Centre in Scotland joining the royal tour.
As the King left the Bahamas on Thursday to fly to Guyana for the second leg of his Caribbean tour, his spokesman said the islands had "a special place in the King's heart."
"The great wall of cheers he received when greeting crowds will echo long in his memory - and be a source of tremendous pride and encouragement as the tour continues to Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda."
The two day trip to the Bahamas saw the King meet young boxers, environmentalists and politicians.
He also joined the dancing in a Junkanoo parade to celebrate island life.
But in his only public speech of the tour so far, delivered during his first engagement in the Bahamas, the King referenced the UK's involvement in the slave trade acknowledging the "suffering of the past."
His spokesman said: "The King had hoped, the visit proved an opportunity to celebrate and reaffirm the modern partnership between The Bahamas and the UK. And to address the shared challenges of the future and also to acknowledge the great injustices of the past in a respectful way."
The tour comes amidst renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in the slave trade and to offer reparations - compensation from those countries who profited from the trade in enslaved men and women.
A small number of protesters were at some of the King's engagements in the Bahamas, with campaigners holding signs saying "pay us what you owe us" but their presence did not disrupt events.
The Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting (CHOGM) being held in Antigua and Barbuda from 1 November will discuss the legacy of slavery. The King will deliver a speech as Head of the Commonwealth.
