articles.title_orig: SpaceX’s Largest Revenue Source Is a Finite Deal With Anthropic
articles.title_zh: SpaceX’s Largest Revenue Source Is a Finite Deal With Anthropic
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic faces intense competitive pressure and huge fixed costs. Can Claude build itself fast enough to succeed?
Anthropic faces intense competitive pressure and huge fixed costs. Can Claude build itself fast enough to succeed?
The Anthropic S-1 seems to have provided the financial justification for the company to spend as much as it possibly can on compute. If you are the kind of person who wonders if Anthropic is doing its level best to build a machine god while convincing Wall Street it’s in the business of selling IT contracts, Anthropic has just offered a handy solution: Doing a bunch of things that look like you’re trying to build the machine god is the only way to avoid going bankrupt.
Forget about the machine god for a minute. At least in my read of the S-1, it seems like Anthropic is pinning the future of its company to dramatic growth; it has to, in order to meet its fixed costs. You don’t have to be an AI skeptic to lift an eyebrow at these numbers. But if you are skeptical that dramatic recursive self-improvement is possible — in the way the business plan seems to require — this doesn’t look like a good investment.
Let’s start with the good news for Anthropic fans. The company’s revenue grew fourteen times to $16.3 billion between the first half of 2026 and the first half of 2025. There’s an $80 billion loss, but it’s largely an accounting thing that isn’t relevant to the underlying business . If we remove that, and some other charges, including employee compensation, we’re looking at $1.62 billion in adjusted income in the first half of 2026. I’ve asked before if AI can make enough money to pay for itself , and the answer from Anthropic’s S-1 appears to be, at least for this company, at least right now, yes.
Anthropic names only OpenAI and Google as rivals
Anthropic was considerably more disciplined than OpenAI or Elon Musk, and it seems to be paying off. (Anthropic names only OpenAI and Google as rivals. Better luck next time, Elon!) The company has never released an AI image generator, an AI TikTok clone, or an AI waifu. Instead, it specialized in tasks like coding and cybersecurity, staying laser-focused on the thing it is easiest for a computer to do: more computer. And it focused on the enterprise market, which is less fickle than consumers. Its net revenue retention is 900 percent. Pretty good! That revenue isn’t consumers, either. About three-quarters of customers in the first half of 2026 are spending at least $100,000 a year.
On the other hand, Anthropic is under intense competitive pressure — from both other frontier labs and open-source models. The other frontier labs are all rushing for the cutting edge, too. Claude Opus 5.5 currently sits atop the Epoch Capabilities Index , but that leaderboard changes frequently. And for anyone who doesn’t care that their software is four months behind , there are the open-source ones.
What’s more, Anthropic has a disadvantage against a rival like Google. It doesn’t have multiple paths to revenue — and Google does. Google can also wrap its AI into other products businesses already use. Remember when Microsoft Teams ate Slack ? It wasn’t because Teams was the better product; Microsoft just had better distribution, since Teams was bundled with other programs companies were already paying for. Having the best model matters more for cybersecurity — one area Anthropic is targeting for growth — than for instant messaging software, but it’s hard to compete on distribution.
There are some long-term commitments that highlight how intense the expansion pressure is on Anthropic
And also, revenue comes in spurts, usually after a new model is released. Between the competition and growth in use after each novel model, Anthropic can never stop training, and it has to do so more efficiently than its much larger competition.
So one important question is: Can Anthropic continue to provide the results we see in the S-1?
There are some long-term commitments that highlight how intense the expansion pressure is on Anthropic. Sure, there’s a convenient blank on its purchase commitments and lease agreements on page 64, and another kicky little blank on the amounts it’s expecting to spend before December 31st, 2030, on page 137. However, we know the commitments run through 2045.
Fortunately, there’s a “Commitments and contingencies” section that can help us out a little. There’s a fixed minimum of non-cancelable purchase commitments that total $265.6 billion, with terms between one and 20 years. The company has lease agreements “primarily related to compute and infrastructure capacity” that haven’t yet commenced of $321.4 billion, as of the unaudited June 30th figures. After that, Anthropic entered new compute and infrastructure agreements totaling about $245 billion, again with terms between one and 20 years. There’s some other transactions that haven’t yet been finalized, which Anthropic estimates as costing $125 billion to $150 billion. There are also other compute commitments that are variable.
“The S-1 does freeze in time a happy period when their initial models skyrocketed in usage.”
If I add all that up, I’m looking at a minimum of around $850 billion of commitments over the next 20 years, which will rise to about a trillion dollars if the transactions that haven’t been finalized are added in at the current estimated cost. And that’s assuming I’m not missing anything, which I may very well be.
So to meet those commitments, Anthropic’s growth must continue at breakneck speed. Anthropic doesn’t give us a payment schedule for its future commitments, but analyst Harrison Rolfes of PitchBook models it at about $90 billion a year from 2027 to 2030, which means $188 billion in revenue to keep the current ratio of cost to compute stable. “Growth is not optional for this company,” he writes. “The contracts assume it.”
Compute and infrastructure (and a few other items) associated with customers cost $2.3 billion in the first half of this year. Model development (and a few other items) was significantly more expensive; Anthropic spent $9.7 billion on it. But Anthropic simultaneously got more efficient — spending less money on compute to bring in each dollar of revenue, according to Rolfes.
Everyone in cybersecurity has to keep running just to stay in the same place, exactly like Anthropic
Is that a long-standing trend? Hard to say. We don’t have the third quarter numbers in front of us. “The S-1 does freeze in time a happy period when their initial models skyrocketed in usage and they didn’t have enough compute so they are able to charge more for what they had,” says Brendan Burke, an analyst at Futurum Group.
As enterprise software, it makes sense for Anthropic to target companies’ IT budgets. Conveniently, cybersecurity is a place where you will absolutely get your shit rekt if you are not constantly up to date — everyone there has to keep running just to stay in the same place, exactly like Anthropic . Of course, AI is part of the problem; hackers can use it to brute-force stuff they couldn’t do before. Plus, the products themselves are also causing headaches thanks to a partner’s sloppy fuck-up of security protocols around AI agents.
Frontier labs need high-margin products to avoid a race to the bottom on token pricing, notes Burke. That made something else stand out to me: Opus 5.5 reduced customer costs by 40 percent over Opus 5. Now, Anthropic says that lower cost means more usage, which lets the company preserve its margins. If you assume that cost reduction happens every time a new model is released, pretty soon you wind up with tasks at a fraction of the price.
Claude is already building Claude under human direction
This isn’t necessarily an insurmountable problem, in part because increased efficiency doesn’t always slash margins, says Gil Luria, an analyst with DA Davidson. Amazon Web Services and other cloud providers ”have become far more efficient every year and reduce their prices every year and they

articles.title_orig: 'It Hasn't Made Any Difference': Gears of War PS5 Cancellation Fails to Boost Xbox
articles.title_zh: 'It Hasn't Made Any Difference': Gears of War PS5 Cancellation Fails to Boost Xbox
articles.content_orig:
Xbox console sales continue to plummet despite the exclusive launch of Gears Of War: E-Day, as games are pulled from the platform in protest.
Earlier this year, Xbox pivoted from its multiplatform strategy to prioritising exclusive games – albeit with a lot of confusing caveats .
The two titles leading this bold new frontier are Gears Of War: E-Day and Clockwork Revolution, while other Xbox games like Fable and Forza Horizon 6 are still set to come out on Sony ’s PlayStation 5 . It was a puzzling move that felt like performative pandering over sound business logic, in the same vein as capping up ‘XBOX’.
Now, cold data has revealed that Gears Of War: E-Day’s exclusivity hasn’t helped reverse dwindling Xbox hardware sales one bit.
As reported by The Game Business , UK data from Nielsen IQ shows sales of Xbox Series X/S consoles fell 22% in October. Additionally, according to Circana’s Mat Piscatella, there is no increase in US sales either.
Speaking to the outlet, Piscatella said: ‘All of the new programs they’re putting into place, at least in the sales and engagement data that I look at, I’m not seeing [them] have any positive impact. The disc-to-digital program hasn’t changed their sales of new physical software trend at all.
Sign up to the GameCentral newsletter for the latest GTA 6 news, reviews of new games you should play and exclusive analysis of the biggest stories of the week.
‘Saying Gears is going to be exclusive hasn’t made any difference in terms of the hardware trend. In fact, it keeps getting worse.’
He added: ‘[Xbox] took Call Of Duty out of Game Pass on day one. And in the engagement data I’m looking at through our player engagement tracker, basically you lost a ton of engagement on Xbox because it’s no longer on Game Pass, and you got no benefit. It’s really hard to find any signs of positivity or hope on that platform right now.’
Last week, Circana reported that Xbox Series X/S sales in September in the US were down 27% compared to the same period last year.
Just recently, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed Xbox revenue had declined 2% year-on-year in Q1 of the 2027 financial year (ending September 30, 2026). However, she painted this in a positive light, next to a 10% decline a quarter ago. ‘We’re making progress, with a lot more work ahead,’ she noted on X.
In Q1, XBOX revenue declined 2% YoY, compared with a 10% decline a quarter ago, while our accountability margin improved. Minecraft and WoW Forever set records, Call of Duty had its most acclaimed release in more than a decade, and our PC platform revenue grew double digits.…
Gears Of War: E-Day was never going to be a massive seller as the franchise is no longer as popular as it once was during the Xbox 360 era. However, even if Xbox knew this, and is merely using it to create good optics, it’s a concerning decision against the backdrop of widespread cuts within the Xbox division . Developer The Coalition was already hit by layoffs in September, and more are expected next month.
For those who’re asking, yes we delisted Celeste and TowerFall on XBox. We did this to support the BDS boycott
Beyond Xbox layoffs and downward console sales, there’s a growing, negative sentiment against the brand for political reasons.
As noted on Bluesky by developer Maddy Thorson, Celeste and Towerfall have been delisted from Xbox in solidarity with the BDS movement. This boycott has been cited as the reason why several other games haven’t been released on the platform, including the critically acclaimed Big Walk .
All of this, combined with the memory crisis, feels like an insurmountable hurdle for the company as we approach the next generation console race. However, we’ll have to see if GTA 6 will help lift Xbox sales to some degree – despite console shortages.

articles.title_zh: US bans Chinese labs from testing electronics ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
articles.content_orig:
The FCC measure targets testing facilities with alleged PLA ties, giving US labs until December 2028 to expand capacity
The United States on Thursday banned all Chinese laboratories from testing electronic devices destined for the US market, just weeks before US President Donald Trump is due to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) voted to bar testing laboratories and certification bodies in China and other economies that lack a “mutual recognition agreement” or reciprocal trade agreement with the US.
“This is consistent with President Trump’s broader effort to restore balance and fairness with respect to America’s dealings with foreign nations,” said FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.2 adds new video feature that’s perfect for iPhone Duo
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.2 adds new video feature that’s perfect for iPhone Duo
articles.content_orig:
Today, Apple rolled out the 27.2 updates for its operating systems, including iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, and so on.
Let’s start with iOS 27.2. This update is heavily focused on Siri AI. It adds a memory feature to Siri, so it can “recall your past conversations” and reference them when chatting with you. It also expands what data sources Siri can access when giving responses to include voicemails, Messages attachments, and more.
On the flip side, there is now an “Excluded Apps” option that allows you to “choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access.” Further, Siri AI is now available in five more languages beyond English, as previously announced: French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish—though Siri AI remains unavailable in Europe (and mainland China).
Other additions include context-aware suggestions within Messages (like turning a message inviting you to something into a calendar entry), SynthID watermarking support in Photos, and support for user profiles in the Apple TV app. There’s also the new Apple Music branding , plus the arrival of previously promised Apple Pencil support on the iPhone Duo foldable.
The macOS Golden Gate 27.2 offers some of the same things: contextual memory for Siri, the same additional Siri AI languages, and miscellaneous unspecified bug fixes. The same goes for the Apple Watch—again, mostly the same Siri-related updates. visionOS 27.2 includes the new languages and updated Music icon, as well.
Also, as previously discovered in the beta releases of macOS 27.2, there are some references to new gesture recognition capabilities in applications like Photos, Notes, and Safari—which may be related to unconfirmed reports of touch support on the next MacBook Pro refresh, which may be revealed at a scheduled public briefing this Wednesday.
Apple’s own iOS and macOS update notes are below.
Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)
This update provides enhancements to Siri AI with the ability to retain useful context from previous Siri interactions as well as draw from a wider range of personal context. It also introduces Suggestions in Messages that help you take quick actions in apps like Calendar and Reminders based on context from your conversation. This release includes additional features, bug fixes, and security updates for your Mac.

articles.title_orig: Some Polymarket user funds stolen by hackers; exchange referring matter to U.K. authorities
articles.title_zh: Some Polymarket user funds stolen by hackers; exchange referring matter to U.K. authorities
articles.content_orig:
Some users of prediction market platform Polymarket's international exchange had funds stolen from their accounts due to a hack of an unnamed third-party provider.
Polymarket has contacted law enforcement and pledged to reimburse any affected trader. It's unclear how many users were impacted. The company's U.S. platform was not compromised.
Traders first reported on social media platforms that they were seeing unauthorized withdrawals from their accounts on Thursday afternoon. In response, the company halted trading on its international platform.
Polymarket said that it has fixed the issue on its end, and that trading resumed at 3 p.m. ET.
A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the issue stemmed from a hack of DebugBear, a website performance monitoring platform. DebugBear in a post on X said that it was impacted by a security incident on Thursday. The person familiar with the Polymarket outage said that the company referred the matter to U.K. law enforcement, as that is where DebugBear is based.
DebugBear didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
An analysis of publicly-available data by two analytics firms — Betting Intelligence and Polysights — provided to CNBC said that an account on Polymarket Thursday withdrew at least $2.7 million across 710 other wallets.
Polymarket's international prediction market exchange operates as a decentralized finance platform on the Polygon blockchain and is not regulated in the U.S.
The disruption comes just days before both the company's international and U.S. exchanges are expected to see heightened volumes during the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Back in June, a similar incident happened, when Polymarket said a third party vendor had been "compromised" and that the company would refund affected users.

A pair of Gemini app updates today brings the latest design to all Android devices, while file generation sees a big upgrade.
The latest Gemini overlay design applies a heavy blur effect over the bar. It’s hard to make out the boundaries of the pill, while there are way more tiny specks and swirls of color. Once the animations complete, you can see how the pill-shaped bar is translucent at the perimeter instead of a solid shape.
This updated design was first introduced on phones with Gemini Intelligence (Pixel 11) and is now available on all other devices we checked today. Make sure to Force stop the Google app if you’re not seeing it yet.
Meanwhile, the Gemini app now lets you “generate, preview, and edit files right within” chats. You can have Gemini create a text document, presentation, or spreadsheet about a specific topic and then view it inline. Highlight sections to make edits or ask questions.
PDF preview and editing are supported on gemini.google.com and the mobile apps, while Google Docs, Google Sheets, Google Slides, Markdown files, TXT files, and code are web-only.

articles.title_orig: 'Operation Supercharge': Japan and U.S. agree to develop Japanese missile facility
articles.title_zh: 'Operation Supercharge': Japan and U.S. agree to develop Japanese missile facility
articles.content_orig:
From left, Philippines Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, Australia Defense Minister Richard Marles, Japan Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and U.S.Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth prepare to leave after posing for pictures before holding a Quadrilateral Meeting on the sidelines of the 20th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defence Ministers' Meeting (ADMM) and 13th ADMM-Plus Meetings in Cebu, Philippines, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Rolex Dela Pena/Pool EPA via AP hide caption
CEBU, Philippines — The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, the Japanese defense chief said.
It is the latest move by the allies, which have repeatedly expressed alarm over China's growing assertiveness in Asia.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi made the announcement in a news conference Wednesday night in the central Philippine province of Cebu, where he met U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual meeting of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.
Koizumi raised concern Thursday about China's increasing naval activity in southwestern Japan. He said that three Chinese destroyers and a coast guard ship together crossed the Osumi Strait south of the southern main island of Kyushu and headed east to the Pacific Ocean this week. It was the first such fleet configuration his ministry has spotted, he said.
Koizumi said he cited the incident as "an example illustrating the challenging security environment in the region" in his remark at a session Thursday. His ministry will keep watching the Chinese activity with high level of interest, he said. Japan has been accelerating military buildup in southwestern Japan to deter China.
The annual meetings aim to avert a major regional conflict and strengthen defense cooperation. On the sidelines of the meetings, however, the U.S. and China and their allies have often traded criticisms.
The missiles that will be produced as part of a joint effort called "Operation Supercharge" are essential for the F-35 fighter jets, Koizumi said. The two sides agreed to build a final assembly and inspection plant for the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, in Japan, he said. The U.S.-made F-35s are one of the world's most advanced aircraft and are also used by the Japanese military.
During his brief meeting with Hegseth in Cebu, Koizumi said he "shared a sense of crisis … regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before."
"We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means," Koizumi said.
Hegseth renewed the Trump administration's repeated assurances of commitment to help deter aggression in the region in a separate meeting on Wednesday with ASEAN defense ministers, who were led by the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. Like Koizumi, Hegseth did not mention China by name in expressing his security concerns in the region.
"The approach we're taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear," Hegseth told the ASEAN defense chiefs. "Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves."
His message is "clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners," Hegseth said.
Hegseth has assured the Philippines, the oldest treaty ally of Washington in Asia, that the Trump administration will build a robust deterrence against China's increasingly aggressive actions in the disputed South China Sea. Beijing claims the busy waterway, a key global trade route, virtually in its entirety.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles said his country's forces, along with allies like the U.S., will press on with efforts to defend the rule of law despite China's increasing assertiveness, including in the South China Sea. Australia protested last year after a Chinese J-16 fighter aircraft released flares and passed within 30 meters (100 feet) of an Australian P-8 Poseidon surveillance jet over the disputed waters.
"That doesn't deter us from doing what we need to do and that's essentially asserting the rules-based order here in the end of the Pacific," Marles told The Associated Press in Cebu on Wednesday. "Freedom of navigation on the high seas is profoundly important for Australia."
The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, all ASEAN member states, along with Taiwan, also have overlapping claims in the South China Sea. Confrontations have particularly escalated between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and navy vessels in disputed shoals and outlying waters.
Washington has warned that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces, ships and aircraft come under an armed attack, including in the South China Sea.
Beijing and Tokyo have a separate dispute over tiny Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea, with both sides often accusing the other of infringing on their maritime territory.

articles.title_zh: Trump ignored intel on China’s Nvidia spy to protect company’s stock, report says
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China , prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.
after newsletter promotion
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. Megaspeed and customers like it “receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security”.

articles.title_orig: 'Why not? Australia could replicate the Canadian model'
articles.title_zh: 'Why not? Australia could replicate the Canadian model'
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has branded the Coalition “nativist and protectionist” over its resistance to a proposed European Union trade agreement, but Nationals leader Matt Canavan is doubling down and claiming Labor’s $10 billion valuation relies on figures from before Brexit.
Albanese escalated the brawl over the trade pact by seizing on internal Liberal dissent, after this masthead revealed backbencher Alex Hawke warned colleagues in a closed-door meeting that backing Canavan’s tough stance would be “nutty”.
“[Hawke] questioned why it is that Matt Canavan is making determinations without any process in their party room or their shadow cabinet,” Albanese told reporters in Canberra.
“Trade is a good thing. I thought this was resolved in the 1980s under the Hawke and Keating governments and that, since then, there was support across this parliament and across the mainstream political parties.
“This is just an excuse for going down the road of protectionist and nativist politics. Nativist politics is not in Australia’s national interest. We are a trading nation.”
Albanese, who is struggling in the polls and facing increasing criticism on inflation , tried to turn the EU deal into a political test for the opposition. Labor used nearly all its set-piece speeches in question time on Wednesday to argue for the free trade agreement.
In a press conference to spruik the under-pressure government’s agenda, Albanese cited an upcoming APEC meeting between US President Donald Trump, often described as a nativist, and Chinese leader Xi Jinping and said that at that summit “Australia wants to be ... for free and fair trade unequivocally”.
The prime minister’s attack is unlikely to sway Canavan and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. Canavan frustrated his Liberal colleagues by going out early and declaring both parties were against the deal, before the shadow cabinet or leadership group had agreed. But on the substance of the deal, most Liberals agree the proposed agreement locks future governments into the Paris climate accord, shortchanges dairy and red meat producers, and embeds contentious, pro-union labour rules.
Canavan will on Thursday expose what he claims is a “fake figure” of a supposed $10 billion gain from the trade deal. The Nationals leader, who has been needling into the deal in Senate estimates, said the figure was from 2020.
“The fake figures also include the benefits of increased exports to the UK, from when the UK was previously part of the EU, but now that is no longer the case,” he said.
“The dodgy figures were also based on predictions of enormous export increases, which aren’t possible under Labor’s [deal]. It includes a staggering 528 per cent increase in beef and sheep meat exports, an 86 per cent increase in dairy exports, a 113 per cent increase in rice exports, and a 123 per cent increase in sugar exports.
“Labor has misled the public and the Senate to declare a $10 billion so-called benefit, which never modelled the actual outcomes of the worst trade deal in Australia’s history.”
Hawke, a factional opponent of Taylor, told a Liberal-only party room meeting on Tuesday that Canavan had no right to dictate the Liberal position and said voters could see the economic damage caused by the Trump administration’s stance on tariffs and trade.
“If we don’t have our own identity on key economic issues, then the Nationals will dominate us and that will be at our expense electorally,” Hawke told his colleagues, according to sources in the room.
Hawke praised Taylor for defusing the situation when Canavan, a maverick for years before becoming leader, moved unduly quickly. The backbencher added that it would be seen as “nutty” for a free-market party to outright oppose a deal with the world’s second-biggest trading bloc.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft introduces major DirectX Raytracing update, showing higher FPS and 90% lower memory usage
articles.title_zh: Microsoft introduces major DirectX Raytracing update, showing higher FPS and 90% lower memory usage
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft has announced what it describes as the largest update to DirectX Raytracing (DXR) since its introduction in 2018. The new DirectX 12 Agility SDK 1.722 preview introduces Clustered Geometry, Partitioned Top-Level Acceleration Structures (PTLAS), and GPU-driven acceleration structure builds. These features are designed to reduce the processing and memory costs of ray tracing in games with detailed environments and animated objects.
Clustered Geometry divides complex 3D models into smaller groups of up to 256 triangles and 256 vertices. Instead of rebuilding large acceleration structures whenever geometry changes, developers can reuse existing clusters or rebuild smaller sections. PTLAS applies a similar approach to entire scenes, allowing the GPU to update only areas that have changed. This can reduce the workload in open-world games with moving objects, streaming geometry, and complex environments.
Microsoft demonstrated the new implementation using an AMD Radeon RX 9070. In the published example, a scene using traditional acceleration structure rebuilds ran at just 1.2 FPS. Switching to Clustered Geometry increased performance to 79 FPS, approximately 66 times faster. GPU acceleration structure build time dropped from 788 ms to 3.11 ms, while total acceleration structure memory usage fell from 7,519 MiB to 774 MiB.
Microsoft notes that performance depends on scene complexity, configuration, and GPU hardware. The new approach also requires more temporary memory during acceleration structure builds, despite reducing the memory occupied by completed structures.
Microsoft says the features require no new dedicated ray tracing hardware. NVIDIA has confirmed support across all GeForce RTX generations, including RTX 20-series GPUs. AMD currently supports Radeon RX 9000 graphics cards, while Intel lists Arc B-Series graphics and integrated GPUs in Core Ultra 200V and Series 3 processors. Qualcomm plans Snapdragon X2 support during the first half of 2027.
The update also brings NVIDIA’s RTX Mega Geometry approach into a standardized DirectX implementation. NVIDIA’s technology is already being adopted for Gears of War: E-Day, while the new DirectX API provides a common development path for AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA hardware. Microsoft and NVIDIA have released sample projects demonstrating the technology, including a path-traced forest containing more than 60 million plants across 25 square kilometers.
Clustered Geometry and PTLAS are currently experimental features available through DirectX 12 Agility SDK 1.722 preview and Shader Model 6.10. Developers need compatible drivers and Windows Developer Mode to enable them. Microsoft has not announced when the complete DXR update will reach retail status, and the demonstrated performance improvements should not be interpreted as expected gains in existing games.

articles.title_orig: Long Neptune Strikes Again as Ukraine Destroys 2 More Russian Su-34 Bombers
articles.title_zh: Long Neptune Strikes Again as Ukraine Destroys 2 More Russian Su-34 Bombers
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers in a Neptune missile strike on the Marinovka airfield in Russia’s Volgograd region, the Ukrainian Navy reported on October 29.
The strike was carried out with Ukraine’s Neptune coastal missile system against an airfield used by Russian military aviation, according to the Navy.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The “Long Neptune” is an extended-range land-attack version of Ukraine’s Neptune missile, developed to strike targets far beyond the original system’s coastal-defense role. UNITED24 Media previously reported that the upgraded missile was designed for deep strikes at ranges of up to 1,000 kilometers, with a larger body and warhead than the original anti-ship version.
Two Su-34 aircraft were destroyed at the base of Russia’s 11th Composite Aviation Regiment near Oktyabrsky in the Volgograd region.
“Two more Su-34 aircraft are now on the account of the ‘Long Neptune,’” the Ukrainian Navy wrote.
The Su-34 is one of the main platforms used by Russian tactical aviation to deploy guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities, Defense Forces positions, and frontline areas.
Ukraine’s Navy stated that strikes on Russian military facilities are intended to reduce Moscow’s ability to conduct combat operations against Ukraine.
The latest strike follows another major Neptune attack on Russian tactical aviation earlier this month. On October 15, Ukrainian forces destroyed six Russian Su-34M fighter-bombers at the Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region, according to the Ukrainian Navy.

articles.title_orig: At least 14 people killed in Russian attack on Dnipro train station
articles.title_zh: At least 14 people killed in Russian attack on Dnipro train station
articles.content_orig:
A Russian drone struck the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro as people waited to board a train on Thursday morning, killing 14 people.
Another 10 people were wounded in the strike, the latest in a series of Russian attacks on transport and energy infrastructure in Ukraine that have exacted a heavy civilian toll. At least 19 people including two 15-year-old girls were killed across the country on Thursday, authorities said.
“These are deliberate strikes against civilians, brazen in their cruelty, and the Russians are carrying them out right as the humanitarian operation in Oleshky is unfolding,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in an X post Thursday afternoon.
Russia and Ukraine have since Tuesday been observing a ceasefire in the southern region of Kherson brokered by first lady Melania Trump to allow urgently needed humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
“Russia’s signals are clear – they want the war to continue,” the Ukrainian leader said, urging his international allies to apply “appropriate pressure on the aggressor.”
Addressing Zelensky, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was “heartbroken” by the news of the “senseless and indiscriminate” Dnipro attack. “Together with our allies, we must do everything in our power to mount pressure on the aggressor,” she posted on X Thursday.
Earlier, Zelensky described the Dnipro strike as “horrific” and called for more sanctions to deter further Russian attacks.
US President Donald Trump waived a slate of sanctions related to Russian fossil fuel sales earlier this month, angering Kyiv, which has long advocated for tougher sanctions on Russian energy exports.
Russian state media reported on Wednesday that Washington was in talks with the Kremlin to lift sanctions on Russia’s multibillion-dollar sovereign wealth fund almost five years after they were put in place by the Biden administration following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In response, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukraine’s presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, told CNN: “You cannot lift sanctions and then expect the Russians to take any action. Constructive actions must come first, and then everything else.”
Thursday’s victims included two 15-year-old girls killed in a Russian strike on the northern city of Chernihiv. Another three people were killed by a Russian drone strike on a residential building in the Poltava region.
Footage from the Dnipro strike scene shows several bodies strewn across the platform. The head of the hospital where the wounded were taken told local media many of the injured had suffered shrapnel wounds, and four were having emergency surgery.
The recent uptick in Russian attacks coincides with a critical shortage of air defense missiles in Ukraine, where Moscow consistently denies targeting civilians.
On Thursday night, Russia launched an attack on Ukrainian capital Kyiv using ballistic missiles, the city’s mayor said, just hours after Zelensky warned that Moscow was preparing for fresh strikes on the country.
Also on Thursday, an employee of Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant (ZNPP) in Ukraine was killed by a drone, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency, which condemned the attack.
Ukrainian carried out missile strikes targeting two Russian fighter-bomber planes and an “Iskander” ballistic missile launcher, Zelensky said in his nightly address. Moscow is yet to comment on the claim.
Russia had made clear that the pause in the fighting around Oleshky, where thousands have been trapped by fighting without electricity or fresh food and water supplies, applied only to that region.
Both sides have adhered to the ceasefire conditions, which will remain in place until 10:59 p.m. local time on November 1.
CNN’s Billy Stockwell contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
articles.title_zh: Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
articles.content_orig:
Two Russian Sukhoi Su-34 fighter jets were destroyed on the ground during a Ukrainian missile attack deep inside the neighbouring country, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday evening.
"Thank you, guys, for the result," Zelensky said in his daily address, adding that a launcher for Russian Iskander missiles was also damaged in a separate strike.
According to the Ukrainian navy, an attack using Neptune missiles was carried out against the Marinovka military airfield in Russia's southern Volgograd region. The airbase is located more than 450 kilometres from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
This would mark the second successful Ukrainian missile attack on a Russian military airfield in October. The Russian military did not comment on the claims.
However, Russian bloggers close to the military indirectly confirmed the loss. Among others, the blogger "Fighterbomber" wrote: "I hope the realization that the frontline air force must be withdrawn further and deeper reaches the top commanders in time, before there is nothing left to withdraw."
Su-34 jets are used to drop the dreaded glide bombs that have plagued Ukrainian cities since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022. Equipped with wing structures, the bombs are dropped from high altitudes and dozens of kilometres away from enemy air defences to hit their targets.

articles.title_orig: We're raising our price target on Eli Lilly as the obesity-drug boom rolls on
articles.title_zh: We're raising our price target on Eli Lilly as the obesity-drug boom rolls on
articles.content_orig:
As the commercial momentum behind Lilly’s tirzepatide franchise continues, analysts are increasingly turning their attention to new catalysts in the GLP-1 market, including the launch of oral obesity medicines and the recent rollout of a nationwide access program for seniors.
Since the summer debut of the GLP-1 Bridge program for Medicare Part D patients, Lilly executives have consistently pointed to the expanded access the program has offered seniors and the company’s early advantage over chief rival Novo Nordisk.
On Thursday, while detailing a 39% revenue jump for the third quarter, Lilly laid out additional details on how the new prescription pathway is expanding access to GLP-1 medicines.
As it stands, roughly “seven out of 10” seniors participating in the Bridge program are using a Lilly medicine, Ilya Yuffa, the company’s U.S. president, said on a Thursday call with analysts, noting that Lilly’s products have “performed really well” across the program so far.
The remaining share goes to Novo, with the two companies dominating the U.S. market for GLP-1 medicines used to treat diabetes and obesity.
While Lilly has gained a U.S. market advantage over Novo in injectable obesity treatments with its tirzepatide-based megablockbuster Zepbound, the competitive dynamics have shifted with the arrival of the companies’ oral GLP-1 medicines: Foundayo (orforglipron) for Lilly and the semaglutide-based Wegovy pill for Novo.
Analysts’ attention Thursday therefore turned to whether the Bridge program was moving the needle on Foundayo’s launch, which has lagged that of the Wegovy pill since its April debut, roughly three months after Novo’s oral medicine.
According to Yuffa, about 75% of patients entering the Bridge program are opting for injectables, a trend that may reflect the high efficacy bar set by Lilly’s own Zepbound, the executive suggested. Nevertheless, Lilly is witnessing “good growth and uptake of orals and Foundayo as well” through the Bridge, Yuffa said.
Foundayo generated $184 million in third-quarter sales. While the medicine continues to gain share in the oral obesity market, sales fell short of analysts’ expectations, the team at Citi wrote in a note to clients Thursday.
As for the Bridge program’s broader impact on GLP-1 use, Yuffa noted that about 80% of patients using the program are new to incretin therapies, describing what the company sees as a “significant driver of access long-term.”
Reflecting on Foundayo’s U.S. launch, “we’ve made significant progress since last quarter,” Yuffa pointed out on Thursday’s call, noting a recent uptick in consumer awareness thanks in part to a marketing campaign featuring Martha Stewart.
Yuffa said Lilly’s share of new prescriptions in the U.S. oral obesity market is approaching “four out of 10,” which he described as “good progress overall.”
Questions also surfaced during the call about Foundayo’s dose-escalation timeline, with Yuffa explaining that about 25% of patients have reached one of the drug’s maintenance doses, a proportion he suggested is “actually higher than what you see on the Wegovy pill.”
Lilly CEO Dave Ricks also pointed to the opportunity awaiting Foundayo in type 2 diabetes, which he said accounts for “roughly half the volume of GLP-1s” in the U.S. Novo also sells an oral diabetes medication under the Ozempic brand, a reformulated version of its semaglutide-based Rybelsus tablets. The product is distinct from Novo’s Wegovy pill for obesity.
Since its U.S. debut, Foundayo has expanded its reach this year with launches in the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia and Mexico, Patrik Jonsson, president of Lilly International, said.
So far, those international launches have also performed “very much in line with our expectations,” Jonsson said, adding that Lilly is seeing signs that oral GLP-1s are expanding the pool of patients receiving incretin therapies outside the U.S.
In January, Yuffa will step into the newly created role of president of Lilly Global Markets, assuming responsibility for both the U.S. and the company’s commercial operations abroad as Jonsson prepares to retire after 36 years with the drugmaker.
In the third quarter, Lilly generated $24.4 billion in revenue, representing a 39% year-over-year increase and coming in $1.8 billion above consensus projections, according to Citi analysts.
Unsurprisingly, Mounjaro for diabetes and Zepbound for obesity remained Lilly’s biggest growth drivers for the period, with Mounjaro generating $10.7 billion compared with Zepbound’s $5.4 billion. That represented year-over-year growth of 65% and 49%, respectively.
As Lilly maintains its lead in the broader U.S. GLP-1 market, Mounjaro’s sales also benefited from strong growth abroad, the Citi team pointed out. The analysts added that Mounjaro and Zepbound’s continued growth trajectories several years after their launches “remain impressive.”
Other significant contributors to third-quarter revenue included Jardiance, which delivered $1.6 billion, and Trulicity at $904 million. The Citi team said the two medicines collectively gave Lilly “additional cardiometabolic breadth.”
With its incretin business continuing to grow, Lilly raised its full-year revenue guidance to $91 billion to $92 billion, a $5.5 billion increase at the midpoint.

articles.title_orig: Met refers itself to police watchdog over letter about Meghan's father
articles.title_zh: Met refers itself to police watchdog over letter about Meghan's father
articles.content_orig:
The Metropolitan Police has referred itself to the police complaints watchdog over its handling of a letter with allegations against Thomas Markle, which was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.
The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.
Markle has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".
The force said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) "in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex."
The Met added it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".
The letter that will be considered by the IOPC was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Roslyn Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.
The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".
Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason for not visiting Thomas Markle and not allowing him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.
Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".
Confirming that it had referred itself to the IPOC, the Metropolitan Police said it was aware of media reports that it had try to obtain a copy of the letter.
"While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom," it said.
It added that the Met has carried out an initial review in recent days which has led to the voluntary referral to IOPC.
The watchdog will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas, it contained claims of alleged offences.
There are also reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to get a copy from the Sussexes.
Meghan, in a statement last week, said she believed the allegations in the letter "were being investigated".
But the watchdog will have to consider what happened to the warnings.
There are also likely to be questions about what royal officials knew about the letter, which was sent when Meghan was still a working royal, and which was forwarded to the Sussexes' office rather than to her personally.
Jim Gamble, former head of the Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre, previously told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he would have expected the police to have shared any warnings.
"If you get information that comes to you about someone from a foreign jurisdiction who represents a threat to children, there's a well-worn path and generally you'd expect a UK police force to share that information," said Gamble.
"I would have expected the Metropolitan Police to have gone to the FBI to say, 'Look, this isn't proven, it's an allegation, you might want to look at it'.
Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received".
"If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken, why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies," she said.
"I believe those questions deserve clear, transparent answers."
Reports of the Met's handline of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.
Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.
Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims.
Philippine Police have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.
However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.
Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".
Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel's Arab parties
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel's Arab parties
articles.content_orig:
Prime minister claims Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal elections, in which his coalition lost its majority
Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics to cling to power, after he claimed that Arab Israeli parties had used foreign backing to “steal” Tuesday’s election, in which the prime minister’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority.
Netanyahu and his allies called on the internal security service, Shin Bet, to investigate alleged vote buying and other irregularities in Palestinian communities in Israel , supposedly funded by foreign money.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the main opposition bloc, accused the prime minister and his Likud party of trying to derail the election results.
“It’s already clear that Likud and Netanyahu have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election,” Eisenkot said in a video message.
The prime minister’s allegations were quickly disowned by a range of government officials, including police officers and members of the election committee. Netanyahu was also rebuked by the president for “tarnishing an entire community”.
On Wednesday night, the prime minister posted a statement by Likud online , which described the claimed violations as “an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamisation of Israel, and the overthrow of rightwing rule”.
Tuesday’s elections led to Netanyahu’s far-right coalition losing its majority after four years in power. The main Jewish opposition bloc also fell short, however, leaving two Arab Israeli parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, holding the balance of power .
Final results released early on Friday local time showed the pro-Netanyahu bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset and Eisenkot’s bloc taking 48 seats. Joint List and Ra’am won the remaining 19 seats, a historic high for the Arab Israeli community, which makes up about a fifth of Israel’s population.
The prime minister’s attack appeared aimed at stopping the Jewish and Arab opposition from voting together in the new Knesset to oust the incumbent speaker, Amir Ohana, a Likud politician and former Shin Bet official, and advancing their own legislation.
The Likud statement posted by Netanyahu on X said: “It is clear that no Zionist party should cooperate with Ra’am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker through votes bought for cash, and form a government that is dangerous to Israel.”
Opposition leaders lambasted the claims of Netanyahu, 77, who has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.
Yousef Jabareen, the Joint List leader, accused the prime minister of incitement. “Netanyahu was defeated at the ballot box,” Jabareen said, adding that he “refuses to come to terms with the fact that the Arab public voted and decided”.
Eisenkot said any investigation should be conducted “without fear or favour,” and with “the utmost caution”, but insisted it could not be used as a reason to delay the convening of the newly elected Knesset, due to be sworn in within 14 days of the election.
The acting director general of the central elections committee, Dean Livneh, said there appeared to be no basis for the claims. Police officials quoted across the Israeli press said the allegations were groundless, adding that voting had been relatively trouble-free.
The president, Isaac Herzog, called for political leaders to “avoid tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy”.
It was not specified in Likud statements, but press reports said Qatar was the foreign power alleged to have funded vote-buying and voter mobilisation. Majed al-Ansari, an adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, said its government “categorically” denied any involvement in the elections.
The record turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship) appeared to be driven by outrage at routine discrimination and fear that it could become far worse if extremist and openly racist members of the government, such as the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, secured another term in office.
On Thursday, Ben-Gvir called for the arrest of Arab party leaders, and Smotrich demanded they be subjected to Shin Bet interrogation.
Voting in Nazareth, the biggest majority-Palestinian town in Israel, was brisk on Tuesday, with few signs of irregularities, other than apparent ploys by the government and coalition parties to suppress the Arab vote.
Some packets of ballots sent to Nazareth polling stations were in Hebrew alone, rather than in Hebrew and Arabic. Election workers said that monitors sent by far-right parties had attempted procedural ploys to slow down voting but had been largely unsuccessful.
The leaders of the Joint List and the Zionist “Change” bloc have ruled out a formal coalition, but officials from both have discussed the possibility of tactical voting in the Knesset to unseat Ohana, the speaker, and to pass some consensus legislation.
One proposed bill would establish a commission of inquiry into the security failures that helped lead to the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, something Netanyahu has blocked over the past two years.
Ahmad Tibi, a party leader on the Joint List, said Netanyahu was trying to subvert the election results by trying to sabotage a common front between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties.
“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told the Reuters news agency.
Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who is a partner in the “Change” bloc, pointed out the irony of Netanyahu denouncing Qatar for election meddling while the Israeli leader’s own political advisers are being accused of taking Qatari money for promoting the Gulf monarchy’s image.
“This morning, suddenly, when it serves his interests, Netanyahu remembered Qatar and is using it to sow chaos and undermine public confidence in the democratic process,” Bennett wrote on X.

articles.title_orig: Rep. Young Kim Urges Secretary Rubio to Raise China Travel Advisory to Level 3
articles.title_zh: Rep. Young Kim Urges Secretary Rubio to Raise China Travel Advisory to Level 3
articles.content_orig:
Oct 29, 2026 | Press Releases
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, House Foreign Affairs East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee Chair Young Kim (CA-40) sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging the State Department to raise its travel advisory for the People’s Republic of China (PRC) from Level 2 (“Exercise Increased Caution”) to Level 3 (“Reconsider Travel”) in light of the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) ongoing wrongful detention of American citizens.
On October 19, the State Department updated its China travel advisory to warn that Americans face a serious risk of wrongful detention , arbitrary enforcement of local laws, surveillance, and illegitimate exit bans without due process. However, the advisory remains at Level 2 – the same category as allies like Italy, Germany, and the United Kingdom, where risks stem from isolated non-state threats. In China, the threat to Americans comes from the state apparatus itself, making the risk constant and countrywide.
“The United States cannot and will not tolerate a hostile foreign power treating Americans, including Mr. Min Zin and Dr. Youlin Chen, who are currently detained, like pawns to be traded,” said Rep. Young Kim. “The Chinese Communist Party continues to use hostage diplomacy as leverage against our country, and Americans considering travel to China deserve a clear, honest assessment of the risks they face. Raising the advisory to Level 3 would deliver exactly that.”
Chairwoman Kim also urged that specific cases of detained Americans, like Mr. Min Zin and Dr. Youlin Chen, be listed on the State Department’s China travel advisory webpage as a warning to Americans.
This letter builds on Chairwoman Kim’s Subcommittee hearing, “Lives Not Leverage: The Long Arm of China and North Korea’s Repression,” where she pressed for answers on whether the State Department should raise China’s travel advisory.

articles.title_orig: Haiti announces new election dates as 2,000 Salvadoran troops help fight gangs
articles.title_zh: Haiti announces new election dates as 2,000 Salvadoran troops help fight gangs
articles.content_orig:
El Salvadoran military vehicles arrive in the Haitian capital Port-au-Prince
El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti as part of a mission to retrieve four nationals who went missing in the Caribbean country almost two weeks ago.
The "robust deployment" was communicated by El Salvador President Nayib Bukele to the Prime Minister of Haiti Alix Didier Fils-Aime earlier this week, the foreign ministry of El Salvador said in a statement on Wednesday.
Bukele said the soldiers would also assist ongoing "security efforts against gangs in Haiti", the statement continued.
Tensions between the two central American countries have escalated over the disappearance of the four air force technicians working as part of a UN-backed anti-gang organisation in Haiti.
The four soldiers with the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) were travelling back to their base in an armoured vehicle when they were ambushed in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets.
No gang has so far claimed responsibility.
The Salvadoran foreign ministry said the "large-scale operation" was "supported by various countries and international organisations".
Earlier this week, Haiti handed four bodies over to special forces claiming they belonged to those of the missing servicemen, but Bukele said they did not match.
He said one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's military uniform.
Bukele threatened last week in an X post to wipe out Haiti's gangs, saying he will replicate action he has taken in El Salvador, if they did not release the Salvadorans.
In October last year , the UN Security Council approved expanded powers for the GSF to tackle worsening gang violence in Haiti.
The multinational force has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway. More than 5,700 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti this year, the UN says, and armed gangs control much of the capital.
Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of President Jovenel MoÃ¯se in 2021.

articles.title_orig: Here’s How Much You’re Paying for Trump’s Tariffs and Iran War
articles.title_zh: Here’s How Much You’re Paying for Trump’s Tariffs and Iran War
articles.content_orig:
An Iranian flag is seen as missiles and air defense systems are displayed at Baharestan Square in Tehran, Iran, on September 29, 2026.
President Donald Trump’s conflict with Iran has become a political liability for his administration. Since the last U.S. strikes on Iran fell on Sept. 8, Trump has publicly ruled out attacking Iran before the November midterm elections—and promised to end the conflict after them.
Then, rumblings grew that U.S. and Israeli military planners had reportedly drawn up new strike options against Iran, including the possible use of the largest non-nuclear weapon in the American arsenal: the GBU-43/B, also dubbed “the Mother of All Bombs”.
The targets purportedly would be Iran’s nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure, though there are doubts about whether the bomb could penetrate Iran’s most deeply buried sites. According to these reports, Trump apparently is seeking a strike he could present as a military victory and then end the war without appearing to back down.
But such an approach risks triggering a far wider war than Washington intends. Tehran remains unlikely to let Washington end the conflict quickly and, fearing a potential attack from the U.S., could itself strike first. Either scenario could lead to a new round of fighting far more destructive than the last.
Reports of military plans involving “the mother of all bombs” came against the backdrop of two other worrying developments. First, Iran has been escalating its naval attacks, likely in response to increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Notably, two UAE-owned cargo ships, the GFS Pride and the Cape Dao , were struck in the Strait as part of this sharp uptick.
Secondly, diplomatic efforts appear to have hit a wall. In late September, Trump rejected the proposal Tehran had put forward on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly: an end to fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions; the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets; and the reopening of Hormuz within seven days. Instead, Washington insists that Iran must take steps regarding its nuclear program as part of the package, something Iranian leaders say they will only do at a later stage.
The timing of any U.S.-Israeli attack remains uncertain. While Trump has said he will not resume attacks before the midterms, Israel held its election on Oct. 27, a week earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reportedly sought renewed fighting before both elections.
American and Israeli objectives may differ, of course. Trump appears to want something he can portray as a spectacular military victory without having to undergo another prolonged war, while Netanyahu’s rhetoric about “ finishing the job ” suggests more ambitious goals, potentially including toppling the Islamic Republic. Tehran seems to be preparing for either scenario with its own response: a prolonged, region-wide war designed to impose devastating economic costs.
The dominant perspective in Tehran is that the next war must be fought in a way that makes it so costly that a future U.S. president would not contemplate another. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said in late September that Iran “will not stop until we have driven the United States out of the region, punished the aggressor, and established permanent deterrence so that no one will dare attack Iran.”
That logic, should it prevail, rules out a symbolic, tit-for-tat exchange. In Tehran’s view, a limited American strike on Pickaxe Mountain , the fortified nuclear site near Natanz that Trump has repeatedly evoked, followed by a limited Iranian response, would send Washington precisely the wrong message: that it can attack Iran’s nuclear facilities, register domestic political gain, and pay a limited, acceptable cost. Iranian officials have therefore warned that even a symbolic, non-lethal strike would trigger a broad response, denying Trump the quick exit he may have asked of his war planners.
Under this scenario, Iran would target regional energy and economic infrastructure. “In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Ghalibaf has warned . The UAE is particularly exposed: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, has accused it of oil “ smuggling ” in cahoots with U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Rezaei also identified new potential targets: undersea cables, data centers, and AI infrastructure in the region, which he claims are worth “more than $2 trillion.” Ghalibaf subsequently extended the threat to regional governments and investors, threatening that anyone providing “funding, equity, land, or energy” to AI companies that “facilitate military aggression” against Iran “will face coercive action.”
If raising the cost of war is the first instrument in Iran’s calculus, duration is the second. Ali Balali , an adviser to the IRGC’s Aerospace Force commander, suggested Iran would conserve its arsenal in preparation for a prolonged confrontation, rather than expend it early. Two days later, Iranian Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia argued that the enemy’s weak point is a prolonged war.
Timing is a third dimension in Iranian thinking. Iranian military officials have increasingly mentioned the possibility of striking first, preemptively. Akraminia stated that if Iran were to conclude that an attack by the U.S. and/or Israel is imminent, “we will certainly engage in preemptive warfare.” Mehdi Mohammadi , strategic affairs adviser to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, went further, arguing that a successful strategy requires not only striking first but also delivering a decisive blow capable of “changing the balance.” There is thus at least the possibility that Iran might move early, and then fight long.
That could occur due to miscalculation resulting from ambiguous American and Israeli signals: leaked strike plans, carrier and amphibious deployments, and aircraft approaching but not entering Iranian airspace. Military experts in Iran see this pattern as an effort to normalize military activity and regain the element of surprise. Tehran could thus mistake military signaling for an imminent attack and strike preemptively, even though it may not want another round of war.
The fourth element concerns the range of those Tehran would hold responsible in the event of an attack. On Oct. 5 Ali Abdollahi , chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, declared that if the United States acted against Iran “directly or indirectly through Israel,” Iranian forces would retaliate against the United States. The warning carries more weight in the wake of Trump’s decision to openly back Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election. Indeed, some in Tehran interpreted this as a signal that Washington would allow Israel to strike Iran after the midterms. As a result, Tehran has made clear that even were Israel to carry out the attack on its own, U.S. forces and assets in the region would face retaliation.
This interpretation suggests that the scope of Iran’s response to a U.S. strike likely would be far wider. Its conduct in Hormuz since late September offers a preview of how it could broaden the conflict. When the UAE, backed by CENTCOM, kept oil moving through a southern corridor along the Omani coast, the IRGC shifted its attacks from small shuttle tankers to supertankers and stated that vessels using the “illegal corridor” would be “pursued and interdicted across the region.” Strikes followed off the UAE coast and near Qatar. An escalation in the region could drive Iran to go after vital energy and other infrastructure across the Gulf.
Iran’s regional partners also could widen the conflict, although Tehran does not fully control their actions. In Yemen, the Houthis have already opened a second maritime front in the Red Sea, threatening shipping and increasing pressure on Saudi Arabia. articles.title_orig: China leaders demand more loyalty and more initiative
articles.title_zh: China leaders demand more loyalty and more initiative
articles.content_orig:
The top echelon of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) held a four-day session behind closed doors in Beijing this week, with the talks focusing on strict leadership and discipline inside the ruling party.
Xi Jinping , who is both the CCP's general secretary and the head of state in China , signaled he would not only deepen the existing anti-corruption effort , but also ensure that party officials demonstrate more loyalty and more initiative at all levels.
According to the press release published on Thursday, the committee published a resolution praising the leadership and Xi Jinping for "enormous political courage and strong sense of responsibility" in tackling the issues of corruption and the weakening of the Party's governance.
The statement emphasized the need to "consistently advance comprehensive and strict Party leadership."
Kerry Brown, head of the Lau China Institute at King's College London, says Xi wants to minimize potential sources of instability.
Amid the current international tensions and the internal problems in China, including economic difficulties, Xi is pursuing his anti-corruption campaign and by demanding loyalty . "This is just going to intensify because if [the CCP] isn't disciplined and united, the party believes that it will go the same way as everywhere else in the world at the moment and become disunited and unstable," Brown told DW.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Xi also recently spoke of the necessity to identify and remove "two-faced functionaries" from the political system.
In his speech, which was published in mid-October by the party's Qiushi Magazine, Xi referred to people professing loyalty to the central leadership while working against its instructions and following their own "individualistic" goals. The Chinese president described them as "political opportunists." He also criticized party officials pretending to be "nice guys," as in, those who use harmony as an excuse to stand aside when problems arise.
Brown points out that China's political system is now facing a crucial dilemma: If officials at all levels are now indeed expected to show innovation and courage in solving problems, the party's control could grow weak. This could, in turn, boost corruption.
However, if CCP leaders lean more on the "strict Party leadership" aspect and ramp up the pressure on the rank-and-file, there is also the danger of suppressing initiative. This could go beyond the party itself and could even affect the military.
The party is "very, very risk averse," Brown points out.
Chong Ja Ian, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore , notes that party functionaries under Xi only have a limited space to make their own decisions.
Taking this into account, the party's push for individuals to show initiative is not necessarily a major issue.
"I believe Xi would like for the officials to act proactively and decisively by conducting specific tasks; but he still doesn't want them thinking for themselves so much that they can question the agenda he prescribed. The 'proactivity' demanded by Xi is limited to the implementation, not decision-making," he told DW.
Brown adds that Xi seems to be ready to sacrifice a certain amount of operational flexibility to gain more control and stability.
"As long as you have unity, you live for another day, right? But if you have disunity, you probably die the same day," he told DW.
This approach "kind of works," at least at the moment, he added.
"It's not like the Chinese economy is disastrous. It's not great, but it's not disastrous. In any case, look at the outside world. It's a mess."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Outside observers are also focusing on Xi's future and possible successors for the 73-year-old leader .
For now, Xi seems to be firmly in control. It is highly likely that he would be confirmed as the party's general secretary next fall, and could stay in that position until 2032.
This is due to the changes pushed by Xi in 2018 , which removed term limits for state and party leaders.
Both analysts told DW that the issue of succession plays a major role in Xi's push towards internal stability.
"There's always a danger of differences in the party fragmenting it, especially when the question of succession comes up," says Brown. "And even though we don't expect to see a successor anytime soon, you know, there's going to be speculation about who might succeed Xi."
"He can't go on forever," he added.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Political scientist Chong Ja Ian says that Xi currently holds all the power. Therefore, the CCP leader could be afraid of his authority being undermined if he named a successor ahead of time.
"On the other hand, a failure to make preparations on time could create a power vacuum that can cause major instability," he told DW. "To solve this dilemma, the current leader needs to have both the necessary self-confidence and the readiness to take a step back — just like his predecessors did. But not everyone has that kind of confidence."
This text was originally published in Chinese.

articles.title_orig: China's PIPL at 5: Enforcement, evolution and what comes next
articles.title_zh: China's PIPL at 5: Enforcement, evolution and what comes next
articles.content_orig:
CIPP/E, CIPP/US, CIPM, FIP
Senior information governance officer
Beyond Change Advisory, Hong Kong China Network Security Association
In 2023, the fifth anniversary of the EU General Data Protection Regulation's implementation led to widespread reflection on its effectiveness, faults and international influence. The international cascade of regulations that followed the GDPR's introduction bolstered the idea of the Brussels effect, the phenomenon through which regulation within the European market influences global standards.
One of the most prominent examples is China's Personal Information Protection Law , which shares many of the GDPR's fundamental concepts. Effective 1 Nov. 2021, the PIPL now celebrates its fifth anniversary.
Comparable concepts include their respective principles, definitions of personal data and information and the roles and obligations of data handlers, the PIPL's equivalent to the GDPR's "controllers."
While these comparable approaches may make it easier for organizations to harmonize their operations, the two laws are not like-for-like. Among the most notable deviations is the Chinese approach to lawful bases. The PIPL does not contain an equivalent to Europe's "legitimate interests" basis, with consent relied upon far more heavily.
Now that the PIPL has had time to develop, the law's fifth anniversary provides its own opportunity for reflection on guidance and enforcement under the law to date.
Enforcement mainly comes under the remit of the Cyberspace Administration of China, though other authorities also contribute, primarily the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and Ministry of Public Security and certain sectoral regulators.
While landmark cases are handled by the CAC, enforcement actions involving mobile apps are often addressed by different authorities. Civil litigation has also emerged as a means for challenging unlawful processing, with multiple "guiding cases" now identified, providing greater clarity on specific PIPL compliance requirements.
